# Part 13 — Spring Core: IoC, Dependency Injection & Beans

> **Important:** Q1–266 are already covered. This section starts at **Q267** and contains only new Spring Core questions.

---

## Section A — Spring Fundamentals

### $\color{red}{\text{Q267. What is Spring Framework?}}$

### Interview Answer

Spring is a Java framework that provides infrastructure for building enterprise applications, with major capabilities around:

```text
IoC / Dependency Injection
AOP
Transaction management
Web development
Data access
Security integration
Testing
```

The central concept in Spring Core is:

```text
Inversion of Control
        ↓
Spring Container
        ↓
Creates and manages objects
        ↓
Injects dependencies
```

Instead of application code manually creating every dependency:

```java
OrderService service =
        new OrderService(
            new OrderRepository()
        );
```

Spring can manage these objects for you.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q268. What is Inversion of Control (IoC)?}}$

IoC means the responsibility for creating and managing objects is transferred from application code to a framework/container.

### Without IoC

```java
class OrderService {

    private OrderRepository repository =
            new OrderRepository();
}
```

`OrderService` controls dependency creation.

### With IoC

```java
class OrderService {

    private final OrderRepository repository;

    public OrderService(
            OrderRepository repository) {

        this.repository = repository;
    }
}
```

Spring creates both objects and provides the repository to the service.

```text
Spring Container
      ↓
creates Repository
      ↓
creates Service
      ↓
injects Repository
```

### ⭐ Interview Point

> IoC is the broader principle; Dependency Injection is one of the main ways Spring implements IoC.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q269. What is Dependency Injection (DI)?}}$

Dependency Injection means supplying an object's required dependencies from outside rather than having the object create them itself.

Example:

```java
@Service
class OrderService {

    private final OrderRepository repository;

    public OrderService(OrderRepository repository) {
        this.repository = repository;
    }
}
```

Spring provides:

```text
OrderRepository
      ↓
OrderService
```

### Benefits

```text
Loose coupling
Testability
Maintainability
Replaceable implementations
Better separation of responsibilities
```

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q270. What are the different types of Dependency Injection in Spring?}}$

Three commonly discussed forms:

```text
Constructor Injection
Setter Injection
Field Injection
```

### Constructor

```java
@Service
class OrderService {

    private final OrderRepository repository;

    public OrderService(OrderRepository repository) {
        this.repository = repository;
    }
}
```

### Setter

```java
@Service
class OrderService {

    private OrderRepository repository;

    @Autowired
    public void setRepository(
            OrderRepository repository) {

        this.repository = repository;
    }
}
```

### Field

```java
@Service
class OrderService {

    @Autowired
    private OrderRepository repository;
}
```

### ⭐ Recommended

For required dependencies:

> **Constructor injection is generally preferred.**

Reasons:

```text
Dependency is explicit
Can use final fields
Object cannot exist without required dependency
Easier unit testing
Better immutability
```

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q271. Why is constructor injection preferred over field injection?}}$

Consider:

```java
@Service
class OrderService {

    @Autowired
    private OrderRepository repository;
}
```

The dependency is hidden inside the class.

With constructor injection:

```java
@Service
class OrderService {

    private final OrderRepository repository;

    OrderService(OrderRepository repository) {
        this.repository = repository;
    }
}
```

Advantages:

```text
1. Required dependencies are explicit
2. Supports final fields
3. Easier unit testing
4. Prevents partially initialized objects
5. Works naturally without reflection-based field injection
6. Makes constructor dependencies visible
```

Testing becomes straightforward:

```java
OrderRepository repository =
        mock(OrderRepository.class);

OrderService service =
        new OrderService(repository);
```

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q272. What is the Spring IoC Container?}}$

The IoC container is responsible for managing Spring beans.

It handles things such as:

```text
Object creation
Dependency injection
Bean lifecycle
Configuration
Bean scopes
Post-processing
```

Conceptually:

```text
Application
    ↓
Spring Container
    ├── OrderService
    ├── OrderRepository
    ├── PaymentService
    └── EmailService
```

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q273. What are BeanFactory and ApplicationContext?}}$

Both are Spring IoC container interfaces.

### BeanFactory

Provides basic bean-management functionality.

### ApplicationContext

Provides BeanFactory capabilities plus many enterprise-oriented features such as:

```text
Event publication
Internationalization
Resource loading
Environment/property access
Automatic post-processor handling
Integration support
```

### ⭐ Interview Answer

> `ApplicationContext` is the commonly used Spring container in application development, while `BeanFactory` provides the lower-level IoC container functionality.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q274. What is a Spring Bean?}}$

A Spring Bean is an object that is instantiated, configured, and managed by the Spring IoC container.

Example:

```java
@Service
public class PaymentService {
}
```

Spring detects the class and creates a managed bean.

You can also explicitly define one:

```java
@Configuration
class AppConfig {

    @Bean
    public PaymentService paymentService() {
        return new PaymentService();
    }
}
```

### Important

Not every Java object is automatically a Spring bean.

It becomes managed by Spring when it is registered with the container.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q275. What is the difference between @Component, @Service and @Repository?}}$

All three are component-scanning stereotypes.

```text
@Component
   ↓
Generic Spring component

@Service
   ↓
Service/business layer

@Repository
   ↓
Persistence/data-access layer
```

Example:

```java
@Component
class EmailClient {
}
```

```java
@Service
class OrderService {
}
```

```java
@Repository
class OrderRepository {
}
```

### Important

`@Service` and `@Repository` are specialized stereotypes of `@Component`.

`@Repository` also participates in Spring's persistence exception translation mechanism.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q276. What is @Configuration?}}$

`@Configuration` identifies a class that declares Spring bean definitions.

Example:

```java
@Configuration
public class AppConfig {

    @Bean
    public PaymentService paymentService() {
        return new PaymentService();
    }
}
```

Spring processes this configuration and registers the returned object as a bean.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q277. What is @Bean and when would you use it instead of @Component?}}$

`@Bean` explicitly declares an object as a Spring bean.

```java
@Configuration
class AppConfig {

    @Bean
    public ObjectMapper objectMapper() {
        return new ObjectMapper();
    }
}
```

Use `@Bean` when:

```text
Third-party class
Custom construction logic
Conditional configuration
Need to configure constructor/factory arguments
```

For your own application class:

```java
@Service
class OrderService {
}
```

is often simpler.

### Typical distinction

```text
@Component
    → Spring discovers the class

@Bean
    → You explicitly provide the object
```

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q278. How does component scanning work in Spring?}}$

Spring scans configured packages for stereotype annotations such as:

```text
@Component
@Service
@Repository
@Controller
@RestController
```

Example:

```java
@Service
public class OrderService {
}
```

If the package is included in component scanning:

```text
Class discovered
      ↓
Bean definition registered
      ↓
Bean instantiated
      ↓
Dependencies injected
```

### Spring Boot

`@SpringBootApplication` includes component scanning behavior through `@ComponentScan` as part of its composed annotations.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q279. What is @Autowired?}}$

`@Autowired` tells Spring to resolve and inject a matching dependency.

Example:

```java
@Service
class OrderService {

    private final PaymentService paymentService;

    @Autowired
    OrderService(
            PaymentService paymentService) {

        this.paymentService = paymentService;
    }
}
```

### Important modern Spring detail

If a class has **only one constructor**, explicit `@Autowired` is generally unnecessary.

```java
@Service
class OrderService {

    private final PaymentService paymentService;

    OrderService(PaymentService paymentService) {
        this.paymentService = paymentService;
    }
}
```

Spring can use that constructor automatically.

---

## Section B — Bean Resolution

### $\color{red}{\text{Q280. What happens when multiple beans of the same type exist?}}$

Suppose:

```java
interface PaymentProcessor {
}
```

and:

```java
@Component
class CardPaymentProcessor
        implements PaymentProcessor {
}
```

```java
@Component
class UpiPaymentProcessor
        implements PaymentProcessor {
}
```

Then:

```java
@Autowired
PaymentProcessor processor;
```

is ambiguous.

Spring can throw an error because multiple candidates match.

Possible solutions:

```text
@Primary
@Qualifier
Inject a collection/map
```

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q281. What is @Primary?}}$

`@Primary` tells Spring which bean should be preferred when multiple candidates match.

```java
@Component
@Primary
class CardPaymentProcessor
        implements PaymentProcessor {
}
```

Now:

```java
@Autowired
PaymentProcessor processor;
```

will prefer:

```text
CardPaymentProcessor
```

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q282. What is @Qualifier?}}$

`@Qualifier` explicitly identifies which bean should be injected.

```java
@Component("cardProcessor")
class CardPaymentProcessor
        implements PaymentProcessor {
}
```

```java
@Component("upiProcessor")
class UpiPaymentProcessor
        implements PaymentProcessor {
}
```

Then:

```java
OrderService(
    @Qualifier("upiProcessor")
    PaymentProcessor processor
) {
    this.processor = processor;
}
```

### `@Primary` vs `@Qualifier`

```text
@Primary
    → default preference

@Qualifier
    → explicit selection
```

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q283. How can Spring inject multiple implementations of an interface?}}$

Suppose:

```java
interface NotificationSender {

    void send(String message);
}
```

Implementations:

```java
@Component
class EmailSender
        implements NotificationSender {
}
```

```java
@Component
class SmsSender
        implements NotificationSender {
}
```

Spring can inject all implementations:

```java
@Service
class NotificationService {

    private final List<NotificationSender> senders;

    NotificationService(
            List<NotificationSender> senders) {

        this.senders = senders;
    }
}
```

Or:

```java
Map<String, NotificationSender>
```

can be injected to access implementations by bean name.

### ⭐ Very useful pattern

This is frequently used to implement:

```text
Strategy Pattern
Plugin-style architecture
Multiple payment processors
Multiple notification channels
```

---

## Section C — Bean Lifecycle

### $\color{red}{\text{Q284. Explain the Spring Bean lifecycle.}}$

A simplified lifecycle is:

```text
Bean definition
      ↓
Instantiation
      ↓
Dependency injection
      ↓
Aware callbacks
      ↓
BeanPostProcessor
(before initialization)
      ↓
@PostConstruct
      ↓
InitializingBean / custom init
      ↓
BeanPostProcessor
(after initialization)
      ↓
Bean ready
      ↓
Application uses bean
      ↓
@PreDestroy
      ↓
DisposableBean / custom destroy
```

### ⭐ Important

This is a simplified conceptual lifecycle. The actual lifecycle includes additional container infrastructure and post-processing.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q285. What is @PostConstruct?}}$

`@PostConstruct` marks a method that should execute after dependency injection and before the bean is ready for normal use.

Example:

```java
@Service
class CacheService {

    @PostConstruct
    public void initialize() {

        System.out.println(
            "Loading cache..."
        );
    }
}
```

Use it for initialization that depends on injected dependencies.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q286. What is @PreDestroy?}}$

`@PreDestroy` marks a method to execute during bean destruction.

```java
@Service
class ResourceService {

    @PreDestroy
    public void cleanup() {

        System.out.println(
            "Cleaning resources..."
        );
    }
}
```

Useful for cleanup of resources owned by the bean.

### Important

Application termination can be abnormal, so don't assume cleanup callbacks are guaranteed under every possible process termination scenario.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q287. What is BeanPostProcessor?}}$

`BeanPostProcessor` allows Spring infrastructure or applications to customize beans before and/or after initialization.

Conceptually:

```text
Bean created
    ↓
postProcessBeforeInitialization()
    ↓
Initialization
    ↓
postProcessAfterInitialization()
    ↓
Final bean
```

This is a very important Spring internal mechanism.

### Why important?

Many Spring features are implemented through bean post-processing.

Examples include infrastructure related to:

```text
@Autowired
@PostConstruct
AOP/proxy creation
Configuration processing
```

The exact implementation path varies by feature.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q288. What is BeanFactoryPostProcessor?}}$

`BeanFactoryPostProcessor` operates on **bean definitions/metadata** before normal bean instantiation.

Conceptually:

```text
Bean definitions
      ↓
BeanFactoryPostProcessor
      ↓
Bean instances created later
```

Whereas:

```text
BeanPostProcessor
```

works with bean instances.

### ⭐ Important distinction

```text
BeanFactoryPostProcessor
    → modifies bean definitions

BeanPostProcessor
    → processes bean instances
```

---

## Section D — Bean Scopes

### $\color{red}{\text{Q289. What are Spring Bean scopes?}}$

Common scopes include:

```text
singleton
prototype
request
session
application
websocket
```

For standard Spring applications, the most important are:

```text
singleton
prototype
```

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q290. What is singleton scope in Spring?}}$

Singleton is the default Spring bean scope.

It means:

> One bean instance per Spring IoC container.

Example:

```java
@Service
public class OrderService {
}
```

By default:

```text
OrderService bean
       ↓
one instance in that container
```

### Important interview trap

Spring singleton does **not** mean:

> Exactly one object for the entire JVM under all circumstances.

It means one instance **per Spring container**.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q291. What is prototype scope?}}$

Prototype scope tells Spring to create a new instance whenever the bean is requested from the container.

```java
@Component
@Scope("prototype")
class ReportGenerator {
}
```

Conceptually:

```text
getBean()
   ↓
new instance

getBean()
   ↓
another instance
```

### Important

Spring manages creation of the prototype bean, but destruction lifecycle management is different from singleton scope. Spring does not generally manage the complete destruction lifecycle of prototype instances.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q292. What happens when a prototype bean is injected into a singleton bean?}}$

This is a common senior-level trap.

Suppose:

```java
@Component
@Scope("prototype")
class PrototypeService {
}
```

and:

```java
@Service
class SingletonService {

    private final PrototypeService service;

    SingletonService(
            PrototypeService service) {

        this.service = service;
    }
}
```

Although `PrototypeService` is prototype-scoped, normal dependency injection occurs when the singleton is created.

Therefore the singleton generally receives **one prototype instance**, which it keeps.

It does **not** automatically receive a new prototype object every time it calls the field.

### If you need a new instance each time

Possible approaches include:

```text
ObjectProvider<T>
Provider<T>
Lookup method
Scoped proxy
```

Example:

```java
@Service
class SingletonService {

    private final ObjectProvider<PrototypeService>
            provider;

    SingletonService(
            ObjectProvider<PrototypeService> provider) {

        this.provider = provider;
    }

    public void process() {

        PrototypeService service =
                provider.getObject();
    }
}
```

### ⭐ Very important interview question.

---

## Section E — Lazy Initialization & Circular Dependencies

### $\color{red}{\text{Q293. What is lazy initialization in Spring?}}$

Lazy initialization means a bean is created when it is first needed rather than during normal application startup.

Example:

```java
@Component
@Lazy
class HeavyService {
}
```

Without lazy initialization:

```text
Application startup
      ↓
Bean created
```

With lazy initialization:

```text
Application startup
      ↓
Bean not created yet

First request
      ↓
Bean created
```

### Advantages

```text
Faster startup
Avoid unnecessary object creation
Useful for expensive resources
```

### Trade-off

The first use may experience initialization cost.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q294. What is circular dependency in Spring?}}$

Example:

```text
A → B
B → A
```

Code:

```java
@Service
class A {

    A(B b) {
    }
}
```

```java
@Service
class B {

    B(A a) {
    }
}
```

Spring cannot construct either object first through constructor injection.

This creates a circular dependency.

### ⭐ Preferred solution

Don't simply try to "make Spring accept it."

Redesign the dependency graph.

For example:

```text
A
↓
CommonService
↑
B
```

Extract shared behavior into another component.

### Senior-level point

Circular dependencies often indicate a **design problem**, not merely a Spring configuration problem.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q295. Why can constructor injection expose circular dependencies more clearly?}}$

With constructor injection:

```text
A requires B
B requires A
```

Spring cannot instantiate either object because both require the other before construction completes.

This exposes the dependency cycle immediately.

That's generally desirable because it makes the design problem visible.

Field/setter injection may allow some circular dependencies to be resolved in situations where constructor injection cannot, but relying on that can hide architectural problems.

---

# Section F — Spring Proxy & AOP Foundation

### $\color{red}{\text{Q296. What is AOP in Spring?}}$

AOP stands for **Aspect-Oriented Programming**.

It is used to separate cross-cutting concerns from core business logic.

Common cross-cutting concerns:

```text
Logging
Transactions
Security
Caching
Auditing
Performance monitoring
```

Without AOP:

```java
public void createOrder() {

    log();

    authenticate();

    beginTransaction();

    // business logic

    commitTransaction();
}
```

AOP allows such concerns to be applied around matching operations.

Conceptually:

```text
Request
  ↓
Proxy
  ↓
Aspect
  ↓
Target method
  ↓
Aspect
  ↓
Response
```

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q297. What is an Aspect?}}$

An Aspect encapsulates cross-cutting behavior.

Example:

```java
@Aspect
@Component
class LoggingAspect {

    @Before(
        "execution(* com.example.service.*.*(..))"
    )
    public void log() {

        System.out.println(
            "Method called"
        );
    }
}
```

The aspect can apply logging behavior to matching methods.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q298. What is a Join Point in Spring AOP?}}$

A join point is a point during program execution where cross-cutting behavior could conceptually be applied.

Spring AOP is proxy-based and primarily supports **method execution join points**.

Example:

```text
OrderService.createOrder()
       ↑
    Join point
```

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q299. What is a Pointcut?}}$

A pointcut defines **which join points should be intercepted**.

Example:

```java
@Before(
    "execution(* com.example.service.*.*(..))"
)
```

This expression selects matching method executions.

Conceptually:

```text
All methods
    ↓
Pointcut condition
    ↓
Matching methods
    ↓
Advice applied
```

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q300. What is Advice in Spring AOP?}}$

Advice defines **what action should be performed** at a selected join point.

Common advice types:

```text
@Before
@After
@AfterReturning
@AfterThrowing
@Around
```

### Example

```java
@Before("execution(* com.example.service.*.*(..))")
public void beforeMethod() {
    System.out.println("Before execution");
}
```

### Around advice

```java
@Around("execution(* com.example.service.*.*(..))")
public Object around(
        ProceedingJoinPoint joinPoint)
        throws Throwable {

    long start = System.currentTimeMillis();

    try {
        return joinPoint.proceed();
    } finally {
        long duration =
                System.currentTimeMillis() - start;

        System.out.println(
            "Duration = " + duration
        );
    }
}
```

`@Around` is especially powerful because it can control whether and when the target method executes.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q301. What is the difference between Pointcut and Advice?}}$

Simple distinction:

```text
Pointcut
    → WHERE should the aspect apply?

Advice
    → WHAT should happen there?
```

Example:

```text
Pointcut:
all methods in service package

Advice:
log execution time
```

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q302. What is a Spring AOP Proxy?}}$

Spring often creates a proxy object around a target bean.

Instead of:

```text
Client
  ↓
Target Object
```

you can have:

```text
Client
  ↓
Proxy
  ↓
Target Object
```

The proxy can perform additional behavior such as:

```text
Transaction handling
Security checks
Caching
Logging
```

before delegating to the target.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q303. JDK Dynamic Proxy vs CGLIB Proxy?}}$

### JDK Dynamic Proxy

Works through Java interfaces.

Conceptually:

```text
Interface
   ↑
Proxy
   ↓
Target
```

### CGLIB-style subclass proxying

Creates a subclass-based proxy around a concrete class.

Conceptually:

```text
Target class
    ↑
Generated subclass proxy
```

### Spring

Spring can use proxy mechanisms based on configuration and the target type. Modern Spring commonly uses class-based proxies where appropriate, and interface-based JDK proxies remain an option.

### Important

Proxy limitations depend on the proxy mechanism and method visibility/finality. This becomes important for self-invocation and annotations such as `@Transactional`.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q304. What is self-invocation in Spring AOP and why is it a problem?}}$

Consider:

```java
@Service
class OrderService {

    public void createOrder() {
        processPayment();
    }

    @Transactional
    public void processPayment() {
        // transaction logic
    }
}
```

If:

```java
createOrder()
```

calls:

```java
this.processPayment();
```

the call occurs directly on the target object.

It does not normally pass through the Spring proxy.

Therefore proxy-based advice such as transaction interception may not be applied to that internal call.

Conceptually:

```text
External caller
      ↓
Spring Proxy
      ↓
createOrder()
      ↓
this.processPayment()
      ↓
Target directly
```

not:

```text
External caller
      ↓
Proxy
      ↓
processPayment()
      ↓
Transaction interceptor
```

### ⭐ Very important Spring interview topic

Common solutions include restructuring the logic into another bean so the call crosses the proxy boundary.

---

# Part 14 — Spring Boot Interview Questions

## Q305–Q342 | 7 Years Experience Level

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q305. What is Spring Boot?}}$

**Interview Answer:**

Spring Boot is a framework built on top of Spring that simplifies the development of production-ready Spring applications by providing **auto-configuration, starter dependencies, embedded servers, and opinionated defaults**.

**Explanation:**

Traditional Spring applications require significant configuration. Spring Boot reduces that configuration and lets developers quickly create standalone applications.

Example:

```java
@SpringBootApplication
public class Application {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication.run(Application.class, args);
    }
}
```

Spring Boot provides:

* Auto-configuration
* Starter dependencies
* Embedded Tomcat/Jetty/Undertow
* Externalized configuration
* Actuator
* Production-ready defaults

⭐ **Interview Point:**

> Spring Boot does not replace Spring. It simplifies configuring and using Spring.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q306. What is the difference between Spring Framework and Spring Boot?}}$

| Spring Framework                               | Spring Boot                           |
| ---------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------- |
| Core framework                                 | Built on top of Spring                |
| More manual configuration                      | Auto-configuration                    |
| Dependencies managed manually                  | Starters simplify dependencies        |
| Usually requires external server configuration | Embedded server available             |
| More boilerplate                               | Convention over configuration         |
| Production features require additional setup   | Actuator provides production features |

**Example:**

Traditional Spring:

```text
Configure DispatcherServlet
Configure component scanning
Configure dependencies
Configure server
Configure database
...
```

Spring Boot:

```java
@SpringBootApplication
public class Application {
}
```

⭐ **Interview Point:**

> Spring provides the underlying capabilities; Spring Boot provides conventions, auto-configuration, and tooling to use those capabilities quickly.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q307. What is @SpringBootApplication?}}$

**Interview Answer:**

`@SpringBootApplication` is a convenience annotation that combines three important annotations:

```java
@SpringBootConfiguration
@EnableAutoConfiguration
@ComponentScan
```

Therefore:

```java
@SpringBootApplication
public class Application {
}
```

is effectively equivalent to:

```java
@SpringBootConfiguration
@EnableAutoConfiguration
@ComponentScan
public class Application {
}
```

⭐ **Interview Point:**

Remember:

```text
@SpringBootApplication
        |
        +-- @SpringBootConfiguration
        +-- @EnableAutoConfiguration
        +-- @ComponentScan
```

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q308. What is @EnableAutoConfiguration?}}$

`@EnableAutoConfiguration` tells Spring Boot to automatically configure beans based on:

* Dependencies present on the classpath
* Existing beans
* Configuration properties
* Conditional configuration rules

Example:

```xml
spring-boot-starter-web
```

When web-related dependencies are present, Spring Boot can automatically configure components required for a web application.

⭐ **Interview Point:**

> Auto-configuration is conditional. Spring Boot does not blindly create every possible bean.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q309. What is @ComponentScan?}}$

`@ComponentScan` tells Spring where to scan for Spring components such as:

```java
@Component
@Service
@Repository
@Controller
```

Example:

```java
@ComponentScan("com.example")
```

If your main application class is:

```text
com.example.Application
```

Spring Boot normally scans:

```text
com.example
com.example.service
com.example.repository
com.example.controller
```

and its subpackages.

⭐ **Interview Trap:**

If your component is outside the scanned package hierarchy, Spring may not discover it.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q310. What are Spring Boot Starters?}}$

**Interview Answer:**

Spring Boot starters are dependency descriptors that group commonly required dependencies for a particular functionality.

For example:

```xml
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
</dependency>
```

This brings the dependencies commonly required for web development.

Common starters:

```text
spring-boot-starter-web
spring-boot-starter-data-jpa
spring-boot-starter-security
spring-boot-starter-test
spring-boot-starter-validation
```

⭐ **Interview Point:**

> Starters reduce dependency-management boilerplate; they don't themselves perform auto-configuration.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q311. What is Spring Boot Auto-Configuration?}}$

Auto-configuration means Spring Boot automatically configures application infrastructure based on the application's environment.

For example, if Spring MVC dependencies are present, Boot can configure the web application infrastructure.

Conceptually:

```text
Dependency detected
       ↓
Auto-configuration candidate
       ↓
Check conditions
       ↓
Create/configure beans
```

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q312. How does Spring Boot Auto-Configuration work internally?}}$

At a high level:

```text
@SpringBootApplication
        ↓
@EnableAutoConfiguration
        ↓
Auto-configuration candidates discovered
        ↓
Conditional annotations evaluated
        ↓
Matching configuration activated
        ↓
Beans registered
```

Modern Spring Boot uses auto-configuration metadata/import mechanisms to discover candidate configurations.

Then conditions determine whether a configuration should apply.

For example:

```java
@Configuration
@ConditionalOnClass(SomeLibrary.class)
public class SomeAutoConfiguration {
}
```

If the required class exists, the configuration can be applied.

⭐ **7-YOE Interview Point:**

Don't simply say:

> "Spring Boot automatically creates everything."

Instead say:

> "Spring Boot discovers auto-configuration candidates and applies them conditionally based on the classpath, existing beans, properties, and other conditions."

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q313. What is @ConditionalOnClass?}}$

`@ConditionalOnClass` activates configuration when a particular class is available on the classpath.

Example:

```java
@Configuration
@ConditionalOnClass(DataSource.class)
public class DatabaseAutoConfiguration {
}
```

Conceptually:

```text
Is DataSource available?
        |
      YES
        ↓
Enable configuration
```

If the class isn't available, the configuration isn't applied.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q314. What is @ConditionalOnMissingBean?}}$

It allows configuration only when a particular bean does **not already exist**.

Example:

```java
@Bean
@ConditionalOnMissingBean
public MyService myService() {
    return new MyService();
}
```

Conceptually:

```text
Does MyService bean already exist?
        |
   +----+----+
   |         |
  YES        NO
   |         |
Don't       Create
create       bean
```

⭐ This is one of the important mechanisms behind Boot's customization model.

> Spring Boot provides a default, but your application can replace it with its own bean.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q315. What is @ConditionalOnProperty?}}$

It activates configuration based on a configuration property.

Example:

```java
@Configuration
@ConditionalOnProperty(
    name = "feature.payment.enabled",
    havingValue = "true"
)
public class PaymentConfiguration {
}
```

Configuration:

```properties
feature.payment.enabled=true
```

Then the configuration becomes active.

Useful for:

* Feature flags
* Optional integrations
* Environment-specific functionality

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q316. What is an embedded server in Spring Boot?}}$

Spring Boot can package a web application together with an embedded servlet container.

Common servers include:

```text
Tomcat
Jetty
Undertow
```

For example, with:

```text
spring-boot-starter-web
```

Tomcat is commonly included by default.

You can then run:

```bash
java -jar application.jar
```

instead of manually deploying a WAR to an external application server.

⭐ **Interview Point:**

> Embedded server is one reason Spring Boot applications can be packaged and run as standalone applications.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q317. application.properties vs application.yml?}}$

Both can be used for application configuration.

**Properties:**

```properties
server.port=8081
spring.datasource.url=jdbc:mysql://localhost/test
spring.datasource.username=root
```

**YAML:**

```yaml
server:
  port: 8081

spring:
  datasource:
    url: jdbc:mysql://localhost/test
    username: root
```

YAML is often easier to read for hierarchical configuration.

⭐ Functionally, both are configuration formats; the choice is mainly readability/team convention.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q318. What is externalized configuration in Spring Boot?}}$

Externalized configuration means application configuration can be supplied outside the compiled application code.

Examples:

```text
application.properties
application.yml
Environment variables
Command-line arguments
JVM/system properties
External configuration files
```

Example:

```properties
server.port=8080
```

Instead of hardcoding:

```java
server.start(8080);
```

This allows the same application artifact to run in different environments.

```text
Application JAR
      |
      +-- DEV configuration
      +-- TEST configuration
      +-- PROD configuration
```

⭐ **7-YOE Point:**

> Environment-specific configuration should generally be externalized rather than hardcoded into application code.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q319. What is property precedence in Spring Boot?}}$

When the same property is defined in multiple configuration sources, Spring Boot uses a defined precedence order.

For example, command-line arguments generally have higher precedence than configuration files.

Conceptually:

```text
Higher priority
      ↓
Command-line arguments
Environment/system properties
Profile-specific configuration
Application configuration
      ↓
Lower priority
```

The exact precedence list depends on Spring Boot version and configuration source.

⭐ **Interview Trap:**

Don't memorize an oversimplified list as universal across every Spring Boot version. Explain that Boot has an ordered property-source precedence mechanism.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q320. What is @Value in Spring Boot?}}$

`@Value` injects a configuration property into a field, constructor parameter, or method parameter.

Example:

```properties
app.name=PaymentService
```

```java
@Value("${app.name}")
private String applicationName;
```

Then:

```text
applicationName = "PaymentService"
```

It can also provide defaults:

```java
@Value("${app.timeout:30}")
private int timeout;
```

If `app.timeout` is absent:

```text
timeout = 30
```

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q321. What is @ConfigurationProperties?}}$

`@ConfigurationProperties` binds a group of configuration properties to a typed Java object.

Example:

```properties
app.payment.timeout=30
app.payment.retry-count=3
```

Java:

```java
@ConfigurationProperties(prefix = "app.payment")
public class PaymentProperties {

    private int timeout;
    private int retryCount;

    // getters/setters
}
```

Now configuration is represented as a strongly typed object.

⭐ **Why preferred for grouped configuration?**

Compared with many `@Value` fields:

```text
@Value
↓
Good for small/simple values

@ConfigurationProperties
↓
Better for structured configuration
```

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q322. What is Spring Environment?}}$

`Environment` provides access to:

* Properties
* Profiles
* Property sources

Example:

```java
@Autowired
private Environment environment;

String value =
    environment.getProperty("app.name");
```

You can also check active profiles:

```java
environment.getActiveProfiles();
```

⭐ Think of `Environment` as an abstraction over the application's configuration environment.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q323. What are Spring Profiles?}}$

Profiles allow different beans/configuration to be activated for different environments.

Typical profiles:

```text
dev
test
qa
prod
```

Example:

```java
@Configuration
@Profile("dev")
public class DevConfiguration {
}
```

This configuration is active only when the `dev` profile is active.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q324. What is @Profile?}}$

`@Profile` conditionally registers a bean/configuration based on the active profile.

Example:

```java
@Service
@Profile("dev")
public class MockPaymentService
        implements PaymentService {
}
```

Production implementation:

```java
@Service
@Profile("prod")
public class RealPaymentService
        implements PaymentService {
}
```

Then:

```text
dev → MockPaymentService
prod → RealPaymentService
```

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q325. How do you activate a Spring Boot profile?}}$

You can activate a profile using configuration:

```properties
spring.profiles.active=dev
```

or command line:

```bash
java -jar app.jar --spring.profiles.active=prod
```

Environment variable:

```text
SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod
```

⭐ In production, profile selection is commonly controlled externally rather than hardcoded.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q326. How do you manage DEV, TEST and PROD configurations?}}$

A common approach is:

```text
application.yml
application-dev.yml
application-test.yml
application-prod.yml
```

Example:

```yaml
# application.yml

app:
  name: payment-service
```

```yaml
# application-dev.yml

server:
  port: 8081
```

```yaml
# application-prod.yml

server:
  port: 8080
```

Activate:

```text
SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod
```

⭐ **7-YOE Best Practice:**

Don't commit production secrets directly into Git.

Use:

* Environment variables
* Secret managers
* Kubernetes secrets
* Cloud secret-management solutions

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q327. What is Spring Boot Actuator?}}$

Spring Boot Actuator provides production-oriented monitoring and management capabilities.

It exposes information about the application such as:

```text
Health
Metrics
Environment
Application info
Mappings
Beans
```

Typically enabled through:

```xml
spring-boot-starter-actuator
```

Example endpoint:

```text
/actuator/health
```

⭐ Actuator is especially useful for observability and operational monitoring.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q328. What is the purpose of the Actuator health endpoint?}}$

The health endpoint provides information about whether the application is healthy.

Example:

```text
GET /actuator/health
```

Possible response:

```json
{
  "status": "UP"
}
```

Health indicators can check dependencies such as:

```text
Database
Redis
Messaging system
External services
Disk space
```

In Kubernetes, health information can be integrated with probes.

⭐ **Senior Point:**

Distinguish:

```text
Liveness → Is the application process functioning?

Readiness → Is the application ready to receive traffic?
```

Don't blindly expose detailed health information publicly.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q329. How can you expose or customize Actuator endpoints?}}$

Actuator endpoints can be configured using properties.

For example:

```properties
management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=health,info,metrics
```

You can also create custom health indicators.

Example:

```java
@Component
public class PaymentHealthIndicator
        implements HealthIndicator {

    @Override
    public Health health() {
        return Health.up()
                .withDetail("service", "payment")
                .build();
    }
}
```

⭐ **Security Point:**

Don't expose sensitive management endpoints unnecessarily.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q330. How does logging work in Spring Boot?}}$

Spring Boot provides logging support automatically.

A common logging abstraction is:

```text
SLF4J
```

with a logging implementation such as:

```text
Logback
```

Example:

```java
private static final Logger log =
        LoggerFactory.getLogger(PaymentService.class);

log.info("Payment processed: {}", paymentId);
```

Common levels:

```text
TRACE
DEBUG
INFO
WARN
ERROR
```

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q331. How do you configure logging levels in Spring Boot?}}$

Example:

```properties
logging.level.root=INFO
logging.level.com.example.payment=DEBUG
```

This means:

```text
Entire application → INFO
Payment package → DEBUG
```

You can also configure logging through `logback-spring.xml` when more advanced customization is required.

⭐ **7-YOE Point:**

Avoid logging sensitive information such as:

```text
Passwords
Access tokens
Credit-card information
Session secrets
Personal sensitive data
```

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q332. What happens when Spring Boot starts?}}$

A simplified startup flow:

```text
main()
  ↓
SpringApplication.run()
  ↓
Create ApplicationContext
  ↓
Prepare Environment
  ↓
Load configuration
  ↓
Determine profiles
  ↓
Discover configuration/components
  ↓
Apply auto-configuration
  ↓
Create beans
  ↓
Initialize embedded server
  ↓
Publish startup/application events
  ↓
Application ready
```

The exact internals are more detailed, but this is the correct high-level interview model.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q333. What is CommandLineRunner vs ApplicationRunner?}}$

Both allow code to execute after the Spring Boot application starts.

### CommandLineRunner

Receives raw String arguments:

```java
@Component
public class StartupRunner
        implements CommandLineRunner {

    @Override
    public void run(String... args) {
        System.out.println(Arrays.toString(args));
    }
}
```

### ApplicationRunner

Provides parsed application arguments:

```java
@Component
public class StartupRunner
        implements ApplicationRunner {

    @Override
    public void run(ApplicationArguments args) {
        // parsed arguments
    }
}
```

**Difference:**

```text
CommandLineRunner
→ String... args

ApplicationRunner
→ ApplicationArguments
```

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q334. What is ApplicationReadyEvent?}}$

`ApplicationReadyEvent` is published when the application has completed startup and is considered ready to serve requests.

Example:

```java
@Component
public class StartupListener {

    @EventListener
    public void onReady(ApplicationReadyEvent event) {
        System.out.println("Application is ready");
    }
}
```

Useful for:

* Startup initialization
* Triggering post-startup tasks
* Logging readiness
* Integration with operational workflows

⭐ **Interview distinction:**

`CommandLineRunner` / `ApplicationRunner` are startup runners.

`ApplicationReadyEvent` represents an application lifecycle event indicating readiness.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q335. What is graceful shutdown in Spring Boot?}}$

Graceful shutdown means allowing the application to stop while giving in-flight requests/tasks an opportunity to complete instead of terminating everything immediately.

Conceptually:

```text
Shutdown signal
      ↓
Stop accepting new work
      ↓
Allow existing work to finish
      ↓
Destroy/close resources
      ↓
Application exits
```

This is particularly important in:

```text
Microservices
Kubernetes
Load-balanced applications
Production deployments
```

⭐ **Senior Point:**

Without graceful shutdown, deployments can cause:

* Dropped requests
* Interrupted transactions
* Partial processing
* Connection/resource issues

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q336. What are important Spring Boot production best practices?}}$

Important practices include:

1. Externalize configuration.
2. Never hardcode secrets.
3. Use appropriate profiles.
4. Configure health/readiness checks.
5. Add meaningful structured logging.
6. Use metrics and tracing.
7. Secure Actuator endpoints.
8. Configure connection pools appropriately.
9. Use graceful shutdown.
10. Set appropriate timeouts.
11. Handle errors consistently.
12. Use centralized configuration/secrets where appropriate.
13. Avoid unnecessary bean creation.
14. Monitor JVM and application metrics.

⭐ **7-YOE Interview Point:**

A senior developer should discuss not only writing the application but also:

```text
Build
→ Deploy
→ Observe
→ Scale
→ Secure
→ Troubleshoot
→ Shut down safely
```

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q337. What are common Spring Boot startup failures?}}$

Common problems include:

### 1. Port already in use

```text
Web server failed to start.
Port 8080 was already in use.
```

Solution:

```properties
server.port=8081
```

### 2. Missing bean

```text
NoSuchBeanDefinitionException
```

Usually caused by:

* Missing component scanning
* Missing bean definition
* Incorrect profile
* Configuration issue

### 3. Multiple beans

```text
NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException
```

Possible solution:

```java
@Primary
```

or:

```java
@Qualifier("paymentService")
```

### 4. Database connection failure

Possible causes:

```text
Wrong URL
Wrong credentials
Database unavailable
Network issue
Driver problem
```

### 5. Circular dependency

```text
BeanCurrentlyInCreationException
```

Often indicates an unhealthy dependency design.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q338. How do you debug Spring Boot auto-configuration?}}$

Spring Boot provides ways to inspect why configurations were applied or not applied.

A useful approach is to enable the condition evaluation report/debug logging.

For example:

```properties
debug=true
```

This can show information about:

```text
Positive matches
Negative matches
Conditional evaluations
```

You can then ask:

```text
Why wasn't my bean created?
Why was this auto-configuration activated?
Why didn't my custom bean override the default?
```

⭐ **Senior interview answer:**

> I don't debug auto-configuration by guessing. I inspect condition evaluation, classpath dependencies, profiles, properties, existing beans, and component scanning.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q339. What are conditional beans in Spring Boot?}}$

A conditional bean is created only when a specified condition is satisfied.

Examples:

```java
@ConditionalOnClass
@ConditionalOnMissingBean
@ConditionalOnProperty
@ConditionalOnBean
@ConditionalOnMissingClass
```

Example:

```java
@Bean
@ConditionalOnProperty(
    name = "feature.cache.enabled",
    havingValue = "true"
)
public CacheService cacheService() {
    return new CacheService();
}
```

This bean exists only when:

```properties
feature.cache.enabled=true
```

⭐ This mechanism is fundamental to Spring Boot auto-configuration.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q340. How can you exclude Spring Boot auto-configuration?}}$

You can exclude unwanted auto-configuration.

Example:

```java
@SpringBootApplication(
    exclude = DataSourceAutoConfiguration.class
)
public class Application {
}
```

You can also configure exclusions through properties depending on the use case.

Why exclude?

For example:

```text
Application doesn't need a database
but database-related auto-configuration is being triggered.
```

⭐ **Interview Point:**

Don't exclude auto-configuration merely to hide configuration problems. First understand why it is being activated.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q341. What is a Spring Boot custom starter?}}$

A custom starter is a reusable dependency package that makes it easy for multiple applications to integrate a common capability.

For example, an organization might create:

```text
company-logging-spring-boot-starter
```

Applications simply add:

```xml
<dependency>
    ...
</dependency>
```

and receive standardized:

```text
Logging configuration
Common filters
Tracing
Metrics
Default beans
Properties
```

A custom starter commonly consists of:

```text
Starter dependency module
        +
Auto-configuration module
        +
Configuration properties
```

⭐ **7-YOE Point:**

Custom starters are particularly useful in large organizations for standardizing cross-cutting infrastructure.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q342. Explain Spring Boot architecture in a real-world application.}}$

A typical Java backend might look like:

```text
                    Client
                      |
                      ↓
              Load Balancer
                      |
                      ↓
             Spring Boot App
                      |
          +-----------+-----------+
          |                       |
          ↓                       ↓
     Controller               Actuator
          |
          ↓
       Service
          |
          ↓
     Repository
          |
          ↓
       Database
```

Supporting infrastructure:

```text
Spring Boot
    |
    +-- Embedded Server
    +-- Spring IoC
    +-- Auto-Configuration
    +-- Configuration
    +-- Profiles
    +-- Actuator
    +-- Logging
    +-- Metrics
```

A request typically flows:

```text
HTTP Request
     ↓
Embedded Server
     ↓
Spring MVC
     ↓
Controller
     ↓
Service
     ↓
Repository
     ↓
Database
     ↓
Response
```

At startup:

```text
SpringApplication.run()
        ↓
ApplicationContext
        ↓
Configuration + Profiles
        ↓
Component Scan
        ↓
Auto-Configuration
        ↓
Bean Creation
        ↓
Embedded Server
        ↓
Application Ready
```

🔥 **7-YOE Interview Point:**

At your experience level, don't describe Spring Boot only as:

> "Spring Boot reduces configuration."

You should be able to explain the complete lifecycle:

```text
Dependency
   ↓
Starter
   ↓
Auto-Configuration
   ↓
Conditional Beans
   ↓
ApplicationContext
   ↓
Bean Creation
   ↓
Embedded Server
   ↓
Request Processing
   ↓
Actuator / Logging / Metrics
   ↓
Graceful Shutdown
```

# Part 15 — Spring MVC & REST API

## Q343–Q380 | 7 Years Experience Level

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q343. What is Spring MVC?}}$

**Interview Answer:**

Spring MVC is Spring's web framework for building web applications and REST APIs using the **Model-View-Controller** architecture.

For REST APIs, the typical flow is:

```text
HTTP Request
     ↓
DispatcherServlet
     ↓
Controller
     ↓
Service
     ↓
Repository
     ↓
Database
     ↓
Response
```

Spring MVC provides features such as:

* Request mapping
* Controllers
* Request/response binding
* Validation
* Exception handling
* Interceptors
* Message conversion
* REST API support

⭐ **Interview Point:**

> Spring MVC handles the web/request layer; Spring Boot simplifies configuring and running it.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q344. What is DispatcherServlet?}}$

`DispatcherServlet` is the **front controller** of Spring MVC.

It receives incoming HTTP requests and coordinates processing.

Simplified flow:

```text
Client
  |
  | HTTP Request
  ↓
DispatcherServlet
  |
  ↓
Find Controller
  |
  ↓
Invoke Controller
  |
  ↓
Service
  |
  ↓
Response
```

It delegates work to components such as:

* HandlerMapping
* HandlerAdapter
* HandlerExceptionResolver
* ViewResolver
* HttpMessageConverter

🔥 **7-YOE Point:**

Don't say DispatcherServlet directly calls every controller.

It uses Spring MVC infrastructure to determine **which handler should process the request and how that handler should be invoked**.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q345. Explain the complete Spring MVC request lifecycle.}}$

This is a very important senior-level question.

Suppose:

```http
GET /api/users/10
```

Flow:

```text
1. HTTP Request
       ↓
2. DispatcherServlet
       ↓
3. HandlerMapping
       ↓
4. Find Controller Method
       ↓
5. HandlerAdapter
       ↓
6. Controller
       ↓
7. Service
       ↓
8. Repository
       ↓
9. Database
       ↓
10. Service returns result
       ↓
11. Controller returns object
       ↓
12. HttpMessageConverter
       ↓
13. JSON response
       ↓
14. Client
```

For REST:

```text
Controller Object
       ↓
HttpMessageConverter
       ↓
JSON
```

Typically Jackson is used for JSON serialization/deserialization.

🔥 **Interview Point:**

The core mental model is:

> `DispatcherServlet → HandlerMapping → HandlerAdapter → Controller → Message Conversion → Response`

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q346. What is @Controller?}}$

`@Controller` marks a class as a Spring MVC controller.

Example:

```java
@Controller
public class UserController {

    @GetMapping("/users")
    public String users() {
        return "users";
    }
}
```

It is generally used when returning a **view**.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q347. What is @RestController?}}$

`@RestController` is effectively:

```java
@Controller
@ResponseBody
```

Example:

```java
@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/users")
public class UserController {

    @GetMapping("/{id}")
    public User getUser(@PathVariable Long id) {
        return userService.getUser(id);
    }
}
```

The returned object is written directly to the HTTP response body, commonly as JSON.

⭐ **Simple distinction:**

```text
@Controller
→ usually view-oriented

@RestController
→ REST/HTTP response body
```

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q348. What is @RequestMapping?}}$

`@RequestMapping` maps HTTP requests to controller classes or methods.

Example:

```java
@RequestMapping("/api/users")
@RestController
public class UserController {

    @RequestMapping("/list")
    public List<User> getUsers() {
        return service.getUsers();
    }
}
```

It can define:

* Path
* HTTP method
* Headers
* Parameters
* Consumes
* Produces

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q349. What is the difference between @GetMapping, @PostMapping, @PutMapping, @PatchMapping and @DeleteMapping?}}$

These are specialized request-mapping annotations.

```java
@GetMapping("/users")
```

→ Retrieve resources.

```java
@PostMapping("/users")
```

→ Create resource.

```java
@PutMapping("/users/{id}")
```

→ Replace/update resource.

```java
@PatchMapping("/users/{id}")
```

→ Partial update.

```java
@DeleteMapping("/users/{id}")
```

→ Delete resource.

Example:

```text
GET    /users/10
POST   /users
PUT    /users/10
PATCH  /users/10
DELETE /users/10
```

⭐ **Interview Trap:**

PUT and PATCH are not identical.

```text
PUT
→ typically complete replacement

PATCH
→ partial modification
```

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q350. What is @PathVariable?}}$

`@PathVariable` extracts a value from the URL path.

Request:

```http
GET /users/101
```

Controller:

```java
@GetMapping("/users/{id}")
public User getUser(@PathVariable Long id) {
    return service.findById(id);
}
```

Here:

```text
{id} → 101
```

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q351. What is @RequestParam?}}$

`@RequestParam` extracts query parameters.

Request:

```http
GET /users?page=2&size=20
```

Controller:

```java
@GetMapping("/users")
public List<User> getUsers(
        @RequestParam int page,
        @RequestParam int size) {
    ...
}
```

Difference:

```text
/users/101
      ↑
PathVariable

/users?page=2
       ↑
RequestParam
```

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q352. What is @RequestBody?}}$

`@RequestBody` converts the HTTP request body into a Java object.

Request:

```http
POST /users
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "name": "Jay",
  "age": 30
}
```

Controller:

```java
@PostMapping("/users")
public User create(@RequestBody UserRequest request) {
    return service.create(request);
}
```

Conceptually:

```text
JSON
 ↓
HttpMessageConverter
 ↓
Java Object
```

Jackson commonly performs the JSON conversion.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q353. What is @ResponseBody?}}$

`@ResponseBody` tells Spring to write the returned value directly into the HTTP response body rather than resolving it as a view.

Example:

```java
@Controller
public class UserController {

    @GetMapping("/user")
    @ResponseBody
    public User getUser() {
        return new User();
    }
}
```

`@RestController` effectively applies this behavior to all handler methods.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q354. What are DTOs and why should we use them instead of exposing entities directly?}}$

A DTO (**Data Transfer Object**) is an object specifically designed for transferring data between application boundaries.

Instead of:

```java
@GetMapping("/{id}")
public UserEntity getUser(...) {
    ...
}
```

prefer:

```java
@GetMapping("/{id}")
public UserResponse getUser(...) {
    ...
}
```

Why?

### 1. Prevent exposing internal structure

Entity:

```java
UserEntity
```

might contain:

```text
passwordHash
internalFlags
audit fields
```

Response DTO can expose only:

```text
id
name
email
```

### 2. API stability

Database structure can change without changing the API contract.

### 3. Security

Avoid accidentally returning sensitive fields.

### 4. Different request and response models

```text
CreateUserRequest
UpdateUserRequest
UserResponse
```

🔥 **7-YOE Point:**

> Entities represent persistence/domain concerns; DTOs represent API contracts.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q355. What is @Valid?}}$

`@Valid` triggers Bean Validation on an object.

Example:

```java
public class UserRequest {

    @NotBlank
    private String name;

    @Email
    private String email;
}
```

Controller:

```java
@PostMapping
public UserResponse create(
        @Valid @RequestBody UserRequest request) {
    ...
}
```

If validation fails, Spring raises a validation-related exception that can be handled centrally.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q356. What is the difference between @Valid and @Validated?}}$

Both support validation, but they serve somewhat different purposes.

### @Valid

Comes from Jakarta Bean Validation.

```java
@Valid
@RequestBody UserRequest request
```

Primarily triggers standard bean validation.

### @Validated

Spring's validation annotation.

It additionally supports **validation groups** and is commonly useful for method-level validation.

Example:

```java
@Validated
@Service
public class UserService {

    public void find(@NotNull Long id) {
    }
}
```

⭐ **Interview Point:**

> `@Valid` is standard Bean Validation; `@Validated` is Spring's extension and supports validation groups.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q357. How do you validate a REST request in Spring Boot?}}$

Example:

```java
public class CreateUserRequest {

    @NotBlank
    private String name;

    @Email
    @NotBlank
    private String email;

    @Min(18)
    private int age;
}
```

Controller:

```java
@PostMapping
public ResponseEntity<UserResponse> create(
        @Valid @RequestBody CreateUserRequest request) {

    return ResponseEntity.ok(
        service.create(request)
    );
}
```

Invalid input should be converted into a meaningful API response.

For example:

```json
{
  "status": 400,
  "message": "Validation failed",
  "errors": {
    "email": "must be a valid email"
  }
}
```

🔥 Don't return raw framework exception messages to clients.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q358. What is @ExceptionHandler?}}$

`@ExceptionHandler` handles a specific exception within a controller or controller advice.

Example:

```java
@ExceptionHandler(UserNotFoundException.class)
public ResponseEntity<String> handleUserNotFound(
        UserNotFoundException ex) {

    return ResponseEntity
            .status(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND)
            .body(ex.getMessage());
}
```

This prevents repetitive try/catch logic inside every controller method.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q359. What is @ControllerAdvice?}}$

`@ControllerAdvice` provides centralized behavior across controllers.

Example:

```java
@ControllerAdvice
public class GlobalExceptionHandler {

    @ExceptionHandler(UserNotFoundException.class)
    public ResponseEntity<ApiError> handle(
            UserNotFoundException ex) {

        return ResponseEntity
                .status(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND)
                .body(new ApiError("USER_NOT_FOUND"));
    }
}
```

Typical use:

```text
Controller
   ↓
Exception
   ↓
@ControllerAdvice
   ↓
Consistent error response
```

⭐ **7-YOE Best Practice:**

Use centralized exception handling instead of duplicating error-handling code across controllers.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q360. How should you design a REST API error response?}}$

A consistent error model is preferable.

Example:

```json
{
  "timestamp": "2026-09-13T10:30:00Z",
  "status": 400,
  "code": "VALIDATION_ERROR",
  "message": "Request validation failed",
  "path": "/api/users",
  "errors": [
    {
      "field": "email",
      "message": "Invalid email"
    }
  ]
}
```

Benefits:

* Consistent client handling
* Easier debugging
* Better API contract
* Better observability

Modern Spring applications can also use the standardized **Problem Details** approach where appropriate.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q361. What is ResponseEntity?}}$

`ResponseEntity` gives explicit control over the HTTP response.

Example:

```java
@GetMapping("/{id}")
public ResponseEntity<UserResponse> getUser(
        @PathVariable Long id) {

    UserResponse user = service.find(id);

    return ResponseEntity.ok(user);
}
```

You can control:

```text
Status code
Headers
Body
```

Example:

```java
return ResponseEntity
        .status(HttpStatus.CREATED)
        .header("Location", "/users/101")
        .body(user);
```

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q362. What is the difference between returning an object and ResponseEntity?}}$

Returning object:

```java
public UserResponse getUser() {
    return user;
}
```

Spring handles response conversion.

`ResponseEntity`:

```java
public ResponseEntity<UserResponse> getUser() {
    return ResponseEntity
            .status(HttpStatus.OK)
            .body(user);
}
```

Use `ResponseEntity` when you need explicit control over:

* Status
* Headers
* Response body

Don't wrap every response in `ResponseEntity` just because you can.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q363. What are HTTP status codes commonly used in REST APIs?}}$

### 2xx — Success

```text
200 OK
201 Created
202 Accepted
204 No Content
```

### 4xx — Client error

```text
400 Bad Request
401 Unauthorized
403 Forbidden
404 Not Found
409 Conflict
422 Unprocessable Content
```

### 5xx — Server error

```text
500 Internal Server Error
502 Bad Gateway
503 Service Unavailable
504 Gateway Timeout
```

⭐ Important distinction:

```text
401
→ authentication required/failed

403
→ authenticated but not permitted
```

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q364. What is the difference between 400, 401, 403 and 404?}}$

| Code | Meaning                                   |
| ---- | ----------------------------------------- |
| 400  | Invalid request                           |
| 401  | Authentication missing/invalid            |
| 403  | Authenticated but insufficient permission |
| 404  | Resource not found                        |

Example:

```text
Invalid JSON
→ 400

Missing/invalid token
→ 401

Valid token but no required role
→ 403

User ID doesn't exist
→ 404
```

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q365. What is REST?}}$

REST stands for **Representational State Transfer**.

It is an architectural style for designing networked applications around resources.

Example:

```text
/users
/users/101
/orders
/orders/5001
```

HTTP methods describe operations:

```text
GET
POST
PUT
PATCH
DELETE
```

Important REST principles include:

* Resource-oriented design
* Stateless communication
* Uniform interface
* Proper HTTP semantics
* Cacheability where appropriate
* Layered architecture

⭐ REST is an architectural style, not a protocol.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q366. What does stateless mean in REST?}}$

Stateless means the server does not rely on conversational session state stored between requests to understand the request.

Each request should contain the information necessary to process it.

Example:

```http
GET /orders/100
Authorization: Bearer <token>
```

The server can authenticate/authorize the request based on the request and its available backend state.

Stateless does **not** mean:

> "The server has no state at all."

The database can obviously contain state.

🔥 **Interview Trap:**

Stateless refers primarily to **client-server interaction/request context**, not absence of database state.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q367. What is idempotency in REST?}}$

An operation is idempotent if making the same request multiple times has the same intended effect on the server state as making it once.

Typically:

```text
GET     → idempotent
PUT     → idempotent
DELETE  → idempotent
POST    → generally not idempotent
```

Example:

```http
PUT /users/10

{
  "name": "Jay"
}
```

Sending it multiple times should leave the resource in the same intended state.

⭐ **Important:**

Idempotent does not mean:

> "The response must always be identical."

It refers to the intended effect on server state.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q368. What is the difference between PUT and PATCH?}}$

### PUT

Usually represents replacement of a resource representation.

```http
PUT /users/10

{
  "name": "Jay",
  "email": "jay@example.com",
  "age": 30
}
```

### PATCH

Represents partial modification.

```http
PATCH /users/10

{
  "email": "new@example.com"
}
```

Conceptually:

```text
PUT
→ Replace

PATCH
→ Modify part
```

⭐ API semantics depend on the contract, but this is the standard distinction.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q369. What is content negotiation?}}$

Content negotiation allows client and server to agree on the representation format.

Client:

```http
Accept: application/json
```

Server:

```http
Content-Type: application/json
```

Spring uses message converters to serialize/deserialize supported representations.

Example:

```text
Java Object
    ↓
Jackson
    ↓
JSON
```

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q370. What are consumes and produces in Spring MVC?}}$

`consumes` specifies the request content types accepted by a handler.

```java
@PostMapping(
    value = "/users",
    consumes = "application/json"
)
```

`produces` specifies response content types.

```java
@GetMapping(
    value = "/users",
    produces = "application/json"
)
```

Conceptually:

```text
consumes
→ What I accept

produces
→ What I return
```

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q371. What is a Spring MVC Filter?}}$

A Servlet `Filter` operates around the servlet request/response processing.

Conceptually:

```text
Request
  ↓
Filter
  ↓
DispatcherServlet
  ↓
Controller
  ↓
Response
  ↑
Filter
```

Typical use cases:

* Request logging
* Security-related processing
* Headers
* Correlation IDs
* Request/response preprocessing

A filter can apply broadly to requests before Spring MVC handler execution.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q372. What is a Spring HandlerInterceptor?}}$

A `HandlerInterceptor` operates within Spring MVC around controller handling.

Common methods include:

```java
preHandle()
postHandle()
afterCompletion()
```

Conceptually:

```text
Filter
   ↓
DispatcherServlet
   ↓
Interceptor
   ↓
Controller
```

Use cases:

* Request timing
* Authentication-related checks in some designs
* Auditing
* Request context
* Controller-specific cross-cutting behavior

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q373. Filter vs Interceptor?}}$

| Filter                                  | Interceptor                    |
| --------------------------------------- | ------------------------------ |
| Servlet level                           | Spring MVC level               |
| Before DispatcherServlet                | Around handler execution       |
| Can apply to broader servlet processing | Focused on Spring MVC handlers |
| Part of Servlet API                     | Spring MVC API                 |

Simplified:

```text
HTTP Request
    ↓
Filter
    ↓
DispatcherServlet
    ↓
Interceptor
    ↓
Controller
```

🔥 **Interview Point:**

Don't say interceptor is simply "faster" or "better" than filter. They operate at different layers.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q374. What is CORS?}}$

CORS stands for **Cross-Origin Resource Sharing**.

Browsers enforce the same-origin policy. CORS allows a server to explicitly permit certain cross-origin browser requests.

Example:

```text
Frontend
http://localhost:3000

Backend
http://localhost:8080
```

These are different origins because the ports differ.

The backend can return headers such as:

```http
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: http://localhost:3000
```

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q375. What is a CORS preflight request?}}$

For certain cross-origin requests, the browser first sends an `OPTIONS` request to determine whether the actual request is allowed.

Flow:

```text
Browser
   |
   | OPTIONS
   ↓
Server
   |
   | Allow?
   ↓
Browser
   |
   | Actual request
   ↓
Server
```

The preflight may include:

```http
Origin
Access-Control-Request-Method
Access-Control-Request-Headers
```

⭐ **Security Point:**

CORS is primarily a **browser-enforced cross-origin access mechanism**. It is not an authentication mechanism.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q376. How do you configure CORS in Spring Boot?}}$

For example:

```java
@Configuration
public class CorsConfig {

    @Bean
    public WebMvcConfigurer corsConfigurer() {
        return new WebMvcConfigurer() {

            @Override
            public void addCorsMappings(
                    CorsRegistry registry) {

                registry.addMapping("/api/**")
                        .allowedOrigins(
                            "https://frontend.example.com"
                        )
                        .allowedMethods(
                            "GET", "POST", "PUT", "DELETE"
                        );
            }
        };
    }
}
```

⭐ **Security Trap:**

Avoid blindly configuring:

```text
allowedOrigins("*")
```

especially for sensitive APIs.

Also be careful when credentials/cookies are involved because wildcard origins cannot simply be combined with credentialed CORS requests.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q377. What is API versioning?}}$

API versioning allows an API to evolve while maintaining compatibility for existing clients.

Common approaches:

### URI versioning

```text
/api/v1/users
/api/v2/users
```

### Header versioning

```http
X-API-Version: 2
```

### Media-type versioning

```http
Accept: application/vnd.company.user-v2+json
```

Most teams choose one approach consistently.

⭐ **7-YOE Point:**

Versioning strategy should consider:

* Backward compatibility
* Client migration
* Documentation
* Deprecation policy
* Gateway/load-balancer behavior

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q378. What is pagination in REST APIs and how should you implement it?}}$

Instead of returning thousands of records:

```http
GET /users
```

use pagination:

```http
GET /users?page=0&size=20
```

Response:

```json
{
  "content": [
    ...
  ],
  "page": 0,
  "size": 20,
  "totalElements": 500,
  "totalPages": 25
}
```

For very large datasets, **cursor/keyset pagination** can be preferable to offset pagination.

Example:

```text
GET /users?limit=20&after=eyJpZCI6MTAwfQ
```

🔥 **7-YOE Point:**

Offset pagination:

```text
OFFSET + LIMIT
```

can become inefficient for deep pages and can be unstable when data changes.

Keyset/cursor pagination can perform better for large, frequently changing datasets.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q379. How do you design a production-ready REST API?}}$

A strong API design considers:

```text
1. Resource-oriented URLs
2. Correct HTTP methods
3. Correct status codes
4. DTOs
5. Input validation
6. Centralized exception handling
7. Pagination
8. Filtering/sorting
9. Authentication
10. Authorization
11. Idempotency where required
12. API versioning
13. Consistent error responses
14. Logging/correlation IDs
15. Rate limiting where required
16. Caching where appropriate
17. Timeouts
18. Observability
19. Backward compatibility
20. Security
```

Example:

```text
POST /api/v1/users
GET  /api/v1/users?page=0&size=20
GET  /api/v1/users/101
PATCH /api/v1/users/101
DELETE /api/v1/users/101
```

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q380. Explain a complete REST API request flow in a real Spring Boot application.}}$

🔥 **Very important 7-YOE question.**

Suppose the client sends:

```http
POST /api/v1/users
Content-Type: application/json
Authorization: Bearer <token>
```

Body:

```json
{
  "name": "Jay",
  "email": "jay@example.com"
}
```

Flow:

```text
                 HTTP Request
                      |
                      ↓
                  Servlet Filter
                      |
                      ↓
                DispatcherServlet
                      |
                      ↓
                 HandlerMapping
                      |
                      ↓
                HandlerAdapter
                      |
                      ↓
                 Controller
                      |
                      ↓
              @Valid validation
                      |
                      ↓
                  Service
                      |
                      ↓
                Repository
                      |
                      ↓
                  Database
                      |
                      ↓
               Domain/Entity
                      |
                      ↓
                  DTO Mapping
                      |
                      ↓
              ResponseEntity
                      |
                      ↓
             HttpMessageConverter
                      |
                      ↓
                    JSON
                      |
                      ↓
                HTTP Response
```

If something fails:

```text
Validation failure
       ↓
Exception
       ↓
@ControllerAdvice
       ↓
Standard error response
```

Example response:

```http
HTTP/1.1 201 Created
Content-Type: application/json
```

```json
{
  "id": 101,
  "name": "Jay",
  "email": "jay@example.com"
}
```

🔥 **Senior Interview Summary:**

A good 7-YOE answer should connect the layers:

```text
HTTP
 ↓
Filter
 ↓
DispatcherServlet
 ↓
Controller
 ↓
Validation
 ↓
Service
 ↓
Repository
 ↓
Database
 ↓
DTO
 ↓
Message Converter
 ↓
HTTP Response
```

And around that flow:

```text
Security
Exception Handling
Logging
Metrics
Tracing
CORS
Configuration
```
