# Part 25 — Testing for Java/Spring 7-YOE

## Q811–Q860

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q811. What are the different types of testing in a Java/Spring application?}}$

The major categories are:

```text
Unit Testing
Integration Testing
Component Testing
API / Web Testing
Contract Testing
End-to-End Testing
Performance Testing
Security Testing
```

Typical pyramid:

```text
             E2E Tests
           /------------\
          / Integration  \
         /----------------\
        /   Unit Tests     \
       /____________________\
```

### Unit test

Tests one class/component in isolation.

Example:

```text
OrderService
   ↓
Mock Repository
```

### Integration test

Tests multiple real components together.

```text
Service
   ↓
Repository
   ↓
Database
```

### End-to-End

Tests the complete user/business flow.

```text
Client
 ↓
API
 ↓
Services
 ↓
DB
 ↓
External systems
```

🔥 At 7 YOE, don't just know testing annotations. You should understand **what level of test is appropriate for a given risk**.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q812. What is unit testing?}}$

Unit testing verifies a small unit of code independently.

Example:

```java
class Calculator {
    int add(int a, int b) {
        return a + b;
    }
}
```

Test:

```java
@Test
void shouldAddNumbers() {
    Calculator calculator = new Calculator();

    assertEquals(5, calculator.add(2, 3));
}
```

Characteristics:

```text
Fast
Isolated
Deterministic
Easy to run
```

A unit test should generally not require:

```text
Real database
Real Kafka
Real HTTP service
Real payment provider
```

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q813. What is integration testing?}}$

Integration testing verifies that multiple components work together correctly.

Example:

```text
OrderService
     ↓
OrderRepository
     ↓
PostgreSQL
```

Instead of mocking everything, the test may use a real database.

Example with Spring:

```java
@SpringBootTest
class OrderIntegrationTest {

    @Autowired
    OrderService orderService;

    @Test
    void shouldCreateOrder() {
        // test real Spring wiring
    }
}
```

🔥 Integration tests catch problems that unit tests cannot, such as:

```text
Incorrect SQL
Wrong bean configuration
Transaction problems
Serialization issues
Database mapping problems
```

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q814. Unit test vs integration test?}}$

| Unit Test                  | Integration Test           |
| -------------------------- | -------------------------- |
| Isolated                   | Multiple components        |
| Usually mocks dependencies | Uses real integrations     |
| Very fast                  | Slower                     |
| Easy to diagnose           | More complex               |
| No real DB required        | May use real DB            |
| Tests business logic       | Tests integration behavior |

Example:

```text
Unit:
OrderService + mocked Repository

Integration:
OrderService + real Repository + PostgreSQL
```

🔥 Good test suites normally need both.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q815. What is JUnit?}}$

JUnit is a Java testing framework used to write and execute automated tests.

Modern Java applications commonly use **JUnit 5**.

JUnit 5 consists of:

```text
JUnit Platform
JUnit Jupiter
JUnit Vintage
```

Important annotations:

```java
@Test
@BeforeEach
@AfterEach
@BeforeAll
@AfterAll
@Disabled
@ParameterizedTest
```

Example:

```java
@Test
void shouldCalculateTotal() {
    assertEquals(100, service.calculate(50, 50));
}
```

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q816. What is the difference between @BeforeEach and @BeforeAll?}}$

### `@BeforeEach`

Runs before every test method.

```text
Test 1 → setup
Test 2 → setup
Test 3 → setup
```

### `@BeforeAll`

Runs once before all tests in the class.

```text
Setup
 ↓
Test 1
Test 2
Test 3
 ↓
Finish
```

By default, `@BeforeAll` and `@AfterAll` methods are static in JUnit 5 unless a different test instance lifecycle is configured.

🔥 Use `@BeforeEach` when test isolation requires fresh setup.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q817. What is Mockito?}}$

Mockito is a mocking framework commonly used with Java unit tests.

It allows you to create test doubles for dependencies.

Example:

```java
@Mock
OrderRepository repository;

@InjectMocks
OrderService service;
```

Then:

```java
when(repository.findById(1L))
    .thenReturn(Optional.of(order));
```

Verify:

```java
verify(repository).findById(1L);
```

The goal is to isolate the class under test.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q818. What is a mock?}}$

A mock is a test double whose behavior can be configured and whose interactions can be verified.

Example:

```text
OrderService
     ↓
   Mock
 Repository
```

Instead of hitting the real database:

```java
when(repository.findById(1L))
    .thenReturn(Optional.of(order));
```

The test can focus on:

```text
OrderService business logic
```

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q819. @Mock vs @InjectMocks?}}$

### `@Mock`

Creates a mock dependency.

```java
@Mock
PaymentClient paymentClient;
```

### `@InjectMocks`

Creates the class under test and injects available mocks.

```java
@InjectMocks
PaymentService paymentService;
```

Example:

```java
@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)
class PaymentServiceTest {

    @Mock
    PaymentRepository repository;

    @Mock
    PaymentClient client;

    @InjectMocks
    PaymentService service;
}
```

🔥 `@InjectMocks` does not magically create a complete Spring application. It is Mockito injection, not Spring dependency injection.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q820. @Mock vs Spring's @MockBean?}}$

`@Mock` belongs to Mockito.

```java
@Mock
```

It creates a Mockito mock without requiring the Spring ApplicationContext.

`@MockBean` was a Spring Boot testing mechanism for adding/replacing a bean in the Spring test context.

Conceptually:

```text
@Mock
→ Mockito-level

@MockBean
→ Spring ApplicationContext-level
```

For newer Spring Boot versions, bean overriding/mocking facilities have evolved, so always check the Spring Boot version used by the project.

🔥 Don't use Spring context mocking when a simple Mockito unit test is enough.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q821. What is @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)?}}$

It integrates Mockito with JUnit 5.

```java
@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)
class OrderServiceTest {
}
```

It enables annotations such as:

```java
@Mock
@InjectMocks
@Spy
@Captor
```

Without Spring:

```text
JUnit
 ↓
MockitoExtension
 ↓
Mockito test
```

This keeps the test lightweight.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q822. What is the difference between mock, spy and real object?}}$

### Mock

Entirely controlled test double.

```java
@Mock
PaymentClient client;
```

### Spy

Wraps a real object but allows selected behavior to be stubbed.

```java
@Spy
MyService service;
```

### Real object

Actual implementation.

```java
MyService service = new MyService();
```

Conceptually:

```text
Mock → fake behavior
Spy  → mostly real behavior + selective override
Real → actual implementation
```

🔥 Excessive use of spies can indicate difficult-to-test design.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q823. when() vs verify() in Mockito?}}$

`when()` configures behavior.

```java
when(repository.findById(1L))
    .thenReturn(Optional.of(order));
```

`verify()` checks interaction.

```java
verify(repository).findById(1L);
```

So:

```text
when()
→ What should happen?

verify()
→ What interaction happened?
```

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q824. What is Mockito's ArgumentCaptor?}}$

`ArgumentCaptor` captures an argument passed to a mocked method.

Example:

```java
ArgumentCaptor<Order> captor =
        ArgumentCaptor.forClass(Order.class);

verify(repository).save(captor.capture());

Order savedOrder = captor.getValue();

assertEquals("CONFIRMED", savedOrder.getStatus());
```

Useful when you want to verify:

```text
The object constructed by the service
```

rather than merely verifying:

```text
save() was called
```

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q825. What is stubbing?}}$

Stubbing means defining what a mock should return or do.

Example:

```java
when(repository.findById(10L))
    .thenReturn(Optional.of(order));
```

Another example:

```java
when(client.charge(any()))
    .thenThrow(new PaymentException());
```

The test controls dependency behavior.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q826. What is verification in Mockito?}}$

Verification checks whether an interaction occurred.

```java
verify(repository).save(order);
```

Can also verify count:

```java
verify(repository, times(1))
    .save(order);
```

Or:

```java
verify(repository, never())
    .delete(any());
```

🔥 Don't verify every implementation detail. Verify behavior that matters.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q827. What is @Spy and when would you use it?}}$

A spy wraps a real object.

Example:

```java
List<String> list =
        spy(new ArrayList<>());
```

You can execute real behavior while selectively stubbing:

```java
doReturn(10)
    .when(list)
    .size();
```

Use cases are limited.

Prefer:

```text
Real object
or
Mock
```

where possible.

🔥 If you need complicated spying to test a class, reconsider the class design.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q828. What is test isolation?}}$

Each test should be independent.

Bad:

```text
Test A creates data
      ↓
Test B depends on that data
      ↓
Test C depends on B
```

Good:

```text
Test A → independent
Test B → independent
Test C → independent
```

This makes tests:

```text
Parallelizable
Repeatable
Reliable
Easy to debug
```

🔥 A test suite where test execution order changes results is a major quality problem.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q829. What is @SpringBootTest?}}$

`@SpringBootTest` loads a Spring Boot application context for testing.

Example:

```java
@SpringBootTest
class OrderServiceIntegrationTest {
}
```

It can test:

```text
Bean wiring
Configuration
Service/repository integration
Application behavior
```

But it is heavier than a pure unit test.

Conceptually:

```text
Unit test
→ No Spring context

@SpringBootTest
→ Spring context
```

🔥 Don't put `@SpringBootTest` on every unit test.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q830. What are Spring Boot test slices?}}$

Test slices load only part of the application context for a focused test.

Examples:

```java
@WebMvcTest
@DataJpaTest
@JsonTest
```

### `@WebMvcTest`

Focuses on MVC/web layer.

```text
Controller
Validation
MVC configuration
Message conversion
```

### `@DataJpaTest`

Focuses on JPA/repository behavior.

```text
Repository
Entity mapping
JPA configuration
```

### `@JsonTest`

Focuses on JSON serialization/deserialization.

🔥 Test slices provide faster, more focused tests than loading the entire application.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q831. What is @WebMvcTest?}}$

It tests Spring MVC components without loading the complete application.

Example:

```java
@WebMvcTest(OrderController.class)
class OrderControllerTest {
}
```

Typical test:

```text
HTTP request
 ↓
Controller
 ↓
Validation
 ↓
Mock service
 ↓
HTTP response
```

Use `MockMvc`:

```java
mockMvc.perform(
        post("/orders")
            .contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
            .content(json)
    )
    .andExpect(status().isCreated());
```

🔥 Excellent for controller/API contract behavior without requiring the database.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q832. What is MockMvc?}}$

`MockMvc` tests Spring MVC endpoints without starting a real HTTP server.

Flow:

```text
Test
 ↓
MockMvc
 ↓
DispatcherServlet
 ↓
Controller
```

Example:

```java
mockMvc.perform(get("/orders/1"))
       .andExpect(status().isOk());
```

You can verify:

```text
HTTP status
Headers
JSON response
Validation
Controller behavior
Exception handling
```

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q833. MockMvc vs real HTTP integration test?}}$

### MockMvc

```text
No real server/network
Fast
MVC-focused
```

### Real HTTP test

```text
Actual server
Actual HTTP stack
More realistic
Slower
```

Use MockMvc for many controller tests.

Use real HTTP tests when infrastructure/network behavior itself is important.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q834. What is WebTestClient?}}$

`WebTestClient` is a testing client commonly used with Spring WebFlux and can also be used in other supported Spring testing scenarios.

Example:

```java
webTestClient.get()
    .uri("/orders/1")
    .exchange()
    .expectStatus().isOk();
```

Conceptually:

```text
MockMvc
→ traditional Spring MVC testing

WebTestClient
→ especially useful for reactive/WebFlux testing
```

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q835. What is @DataJpaTest?}}$

`@DataJpaTest` focuses on JPA-related components.

Typical scope:

```text
Entity
Repository
JPA mapping
Database interaction
```

Example:

```java
@DataJpaTest
class OrderRepositoryTest {

    @Autowired
    OrderRepository repository;

    @Test
    void shouldFindByCustomerId() {
        // repository test
    }
}
```

It is useful for testing:

```text
Derived queries
@Query
Mappings
Constraints
Persistence behavior
```

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q836. Why use Testcontainers?}}$

Testcontainers allows tests to run real dependencies inside containers.

Example:

```text
JUnit
 ↓
Testcontainers
 ↓
PostgreSQL container
```

Instead of:

```text
Test
 ↓
Developer's local PostgreSQL
```

Benefits:

```text
Real dependency
Reproducibility
Isolation
CI compatibility
Environment consistency
```

Example dependencies might include:

```text
PostgreSQL
Kafka
Redis
MongoDB
```

🔥 For serious integration testing, Testcontainers can be much more reliable than relying on developer-specific local installations.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q837. Why is an in-memory database not always enough for JPA tests?}}$

You might use:

```text
H2
```

for fast tests.

But production may use:

```text
PostgreSQL
MySQL
Oracle
```

Differences can exist in:

```text
SQL syntax
Data types
Indexes
Constraints
Transactions
Isolation
Query behavior
Database functions
```

Therefore:

```text
H2 test passes
      ↓
Production PostgreSQL fails
```

🔥 If database compatibility matters, test against the real database technology, often using Testcontainers.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q838. How would you test a Spring Boot repository properly?}}$

Test:

```text
Entity mapping
CRUD
Custom queries
Constraints
Relationships
Pagination
Sorting
Transactions where relevant
```

Example:

```java
@DataJpaTest
class OrderRepositoryTest {

    @Autowired
    OrderRepository repository;

    @Test
    void shouldFindOrdersByCustomer() {
        List<Order> orders =
            repository.findByCustomerId(10L);

        assertEquals(2, orders.size());
    }
}
```

For DB-specific behavior:

```text
@DataJpaTest
+
Testcontainers PostgreSQL
```

is often stronger than H2-only testing.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q839. How do you test REST API validation?}}$

Example DTO:

```java
public class CreateUserRequest {

    @NotBlank
    private String name;

    @Email
    private String email;
}
```

Test invalid input:

```java
mockMvc.perform(
        post("/users")
            .contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
            .content("""
                {
                  "name": "",
                  "email": "invalid"
                }
                """)
    )
    .andExpect(status().isBadRequest());
```

Verify:

```text
HTTP status
Error response
Validation messages
Field names
```

🔥 Test the API contract, not just the validator implementation.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q840. How do you test exception handling in Spring Boot?}}$

Example:

```java
@RestControllerAdvice
class GlobalExceptionHandler {

    @ExceptionHandler(OrderNotFoundException.class)
    ResponseEntity<?> handle(OrderNotFoundException ex) {
        return ResponseEntity.notFound().build();
    }
}
```

Test:

```java
mockMvc.perform(get("/orders/999"))
       .andExpect(status().isNotFound());
```

Also verify the error structure:

```json
{
  "code": "ORDER_NOT_FOUND",
  "message": "Order not found"
}
```

🔥 Global error handling should have explicit tests because it is part of the API contract.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q841. How would you test a service containing business logic?}}$

Use a unit test.

Example:

```text
OrderService
 ├── OrderRepository → mock
 ├── PaymentClient   → mock
 └── InventoryClient → mock
```

Test scenarios:

```text
Success
Invalid input
Order not found
Inventory failure
Payment failure
Duplicate request
Unexpected dependency failure
```

Example:

```java
when(inventory.reserve(order))
    .thenReturn(true);

when(payment.charge(order))
    .thenReturn(true);
```

Then assert:

```text
Order status
Repository calls
External interactions
```

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q842. How do you test retry logic?}}$

Don't actually wait for long production delays.

Mock the dependency:

```java
when(client.call())
    .thenThrow(new TimeoutException())
    .thenThrow(new TimeoutException())
    .thenReturn(success);
```

Then verify:

```java
verify(client, times(3)).call();
```

Also test:

```text
Maximum retry count
Backoff behavior where practical
Permanent failure
Retryable failure
DLT/fallback behavior
```

🔥 A retry test must verify that permanent failures are not retried indefinitely.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q843. How do you test Kafka consumers?}}$

Test:

```text
Message deserialization
Consumer logic
Business processing
Error handling
Retry
DLT
Idempotency
```

Options:

```text
Unit test
Embedded/test Kafka setup
Testcontainers Kafka
```

For realistic integration testing:

```text
JUnit
 ↓
Kafka container
 ↓
Producer
 ↓
Consumer
 ↓
Database
```

🔥 For critical Kafka workflows, integration tests should validate actual serialization and consumer behavior.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q844. How do you test idempotency?}}$

Send the same request/event twice.

Example:

```text
Event ID = EVT-100
```

Process:

```text
First EVT-100
→ business operation executes

Second EVT-100
→ business operation must not execute again
```

Test:

```text
Process event
 ↓
Process same event
 ↓
Verify business operation called once
```

For DB-backed idempotency, test the actual unique constraint/concurrency behavior too.

🔥 This is especially important for payment/order systems.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q845. How do you test concurrency problems?}}$

Single-threaded tests may not expose race conditions.

You can use:

```java
ExecutorService
CountDownLatch
CyclicBarrier
AtomicInteger
```

Conceptually:

```text
100 threads
   ↓
same operation
   ↓
observe final state
```

Example:

```text
Expected = 1000
Actual = 734
```

This may expose lost updates.

🔥 Concurrency tests can be timing-sensitive, so design them carefully and combine them with deterministic synchronization mechanisms.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q846. What is contract testing?}}$

Contract testing verifies that communication between services follows an agreed contract.

Example:

```text
Order Service
      ↓
Payment Service
```

Contract:

```json
{
  "paymentId": "P100",
  "status": "SUCCESS"
}
```

If Payment changes:

```json
{
  "payment_id": "P100"
}
```

the contract test can detect compatibility problems before production.

🔥 Particularly valuable in microservices where independently deployed services communicate with each other.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q847. What is consumer-driven contract testing?}}$

The consumer defines expectations about what it needs from the provider.

```text
Consumer
   ↓
Contract
   ↓
Provider verifies contract
```

Example:

```text
Order Service expects:

GET /payments/123

{
  "id": 123,
  "status": "SUCCESS"
}
```

Payment Service verifies that it satisfies that contract.

A commonly used ecosystem is Pact.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q848. What is end-to-end testing?}}$

E2E testing validates a complete business workflow.

Example:

```text
Create Order
   ↓
Inventory
   ↓
Payment
   ↓
Order Confirmation
   ↓
Notification
```

It provides high confidence but is:

```text
Slow
Expensive
More fragile
Harder to debug
```

Therefore don't replace unit/integration tests with E2E tests.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q849. What is the testing pyramid?}}$

A common model:

```text
              E2E
             /---\
            /     \
       Integration
          /-------\
         /         \
        Unit Tests
       /-----------\
```

Meaning:

```text
Many unit tests
Fewer integration tests
Even fewer expensive E2E tests
```

Reason:

```text
Unit
→ Fast + cheap

Integration
→ More realistic + slower

E2E
→ Most realistic + expensive
```

🔥 Modern systems may also emphasize contract/component testing, so the pyramid is a guideline rather than a rigid law.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q850. What is code coverage?}}$

Code coverage measures how much code is exercised by tests.

Types include:

```text
Line coverage
Branch coverage
Method coverage
Instruction coverage
```

Example:

```text
100 lines
80 executed
```

≈ 80% line coverage.

But:

```text
100% coverage ≠ 100% correctness
```

A test can execute a line without asserting meaningful behavior.

🔥 Quality of assertions and scenarios matters more than chasing a number.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q851. What is mutation testing?}}$

Mutation testing changes production code intentionally to see whether tests detect the change.

Example:

Original:

```java
return price > 100;
```

Mutated:

```java
return price >= 100;
```

If all tests still pass:

```text
Test suite failed to detect mutation
```

This helps evaluate the strength of tests rather than merely their coverage.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q852. What is a flaky test?}}$

A flaky test sometimes passes and sometimes fails without a relevant code change.

Common causes:

```text
Race conditions
Timing assumptions
Shared state
Random data
External dependencies
Test ordering
Timezone issues
Eventually consistent systems
```

Example:

```text
Run 1 → PASS
Run 2 → FAIL
Run 3 → PASS
```

🔥 Flaky tests destroy trust in CI pipelines and should be treated as production engineering problems, not simply ignored.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q853. How would you troubleshoot a flaky test?}}$

Check:

```text
1. Reproduce repeatedly
2. Check logs
3. Check test ordering
4. Check shared state
5. Check concurrency
6. Remove timing assumptions
7. Control randomness
8. Control timezone/clock
9. Isolate external dependencies
10. Run test repeatedly in CI
```

Instead of:

```java
Thread.sleep(5000);
```

prefer deterministic synchronization or polling with a bounded timeout when testing asynchronous behavior.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q854. How do you test time-dependent Java code?}}$

Don't hard-code:

```java
LocalDateTime.now()
```

everywhere.

Inject a `Clock`:

```java
Clock clock;
```

Production:

```java
Clock.systemUTC();
```

Test:

```java
Clock.fixed(
    Instant.parse("2026-01-01T00:00:00Z"),
    ZoneOffset.UTC
);
```

Now the test has deterministic time.

🔥 Dependency injection isn't only for services—it also makes time-dependent logic testable.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q855. How do you test asynchronous code?}}$

Avoid:

```java
Thread.sleep(5000);
```

Prefer:

```text
Awaitility
CountDownLatch
CompletableFuture
Polling with timeout
Explicit synchronization
```

Conceptually:

```text
Trigger async operation
       ↓
Wait for condition
       ↓
Assert result
```

with a bounded timeout.

🔥 Never create tests that simply "sleep and hope."

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q856. How would you test a transaction rollback?}}$

Example:

```text
Create Order
 ↓
Save Order
 ↓
Payment operation fails
 ↓
Transaction rollback
```

Test:

```text
Call service
 ↓
Expected exception
 ↓
Verify DB state
```

The important assertion is not just:

```text
Exception occurred
```

but:

```text
Database changes were rolled back
```

For transaction behavior, an integration test with a real database is usually more meaningful than a Mockito unit test.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q857. How would you test a database deadlock or concurrency issue?}}$

Use multiple transactions/threads operating on overlapping resources.

Conceptually:

```text
Transaction A             Transaction B

Lock Row 1                Lock Row 2
     ↓                         ↓
Try Row 2                Try Row 1
     ↓                         ↓
       DEADLOCK
```

A robust test can verify:

```text
Deadlock detection
Retry behavior
Transaction rollback
Final consistent state
```

But don't make the entire test suite dependent on nondeterministic timing.

🔥 For database concurrency, integration testing against the real DB engine is important.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q858. What should you mock and what should you not mock?}}$

Good candidates for mocking:

```text
External APIs
Payment providers
Email/SMS providers
Repositories in service unit tests
Kafka clients where testing business logic
Slow/unavailable dependencies
```

Usually don't mock:

```text
Simple value objects
Pure business logic
Code you actually want to integrate-test
The entire system
```

Example:

```text
Unit test:
OrderService + mock repository

Integration:
OrderService + real repository + real DB
```

🔥 If everything is mocked, you may end up testing your mocks rather than your application.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q859. How would you build a testing strategy for a 7-YOE Spring Boot application?}}$

I would divide testing into layers:

```text
                 E2E
                  ↑
          Critical workflows
                  ↑
        Contract / Component
                  ↑
        Integration Tests
                  ↑
            Unit Tests
```

### Unit

Test:

```text
Business rules
Calculations
State transitions
Error handling
```

### Integration

Test:

```text
JPA
Database
Kafka
Redis
Spring configuration
Transactions
```

### API

Test:

```text
Request validation
Authentication/authorization
Status codes
JSON contracts
Exception handling
```

### Contract

Test:

```text
Service-to-service compatibility
```

### E2E

Test only critical journeys:

```text
Login
Checkout
Payment
Order completion
```

### CI/CD

```text
Commit
 ↓
Unit tests
 ↓
Static analysis
 ↓
Integration tests
 ↓
Contract tests
 ↓
Build
 ↓
Deployment
 ↓
Smoke tests
```

🔥 The goal is **fast feedback + meaningful coverage + confidence**, not maximum number of tests.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q860. What does a production-quality testing architecture look like?}}$

A mature Java/Spring application can have:

```text
                         CI/CD
                           |
            +--------------+--------------+
            ↓              ↓              ↓
         Unit          Integration      Contract
          Tests            Tests           Tests
            |               |               |
        Mockito          Testcontainers   Pact/etc.
            |               |               |
            +---------------+---------------+
                            ↓
                         E2E Tests
                            ↓
                       Deployment
                            ↓
                       Smoke Tests
```

For a Spring Boot microservice:

```text
Controller
   ↓
@WebMvcTest
   ↓
Service
   ↓
JUnit + Mockito
   ↓
Repository
   ↓
@DataJpaTest
   ↓
Real DB/Testcontainers
   ↓
Kafka
   ↓
Integration tests
   ↓
Contract tests
   ↓
Critical E2E
```

### Production-quality principles

```text
Fast unit tests
Focused integration tests
Real dependency testing where important
Deterministic tests
Independent tests
Meaningful assertions
Controlled test data
Reliable CI
Minimal flaky tests
Security-sensitive tests
Performance tests for critical paths
```

### Senior-level mindset

Don't ask:

> "How can I get 90% coverage?"

Ask:

> "What failures are expensive for this system, and which tests give us confidence that those failures won't reach production?"

That is the difference between **writing tests** and **designing a testing strategy**.

---

# ⭐ Testing Mental Model

When an interviewer gives you a feature, think:

```text
             WHAT AM I TESTING?
                     ↓
        +------------+------------+
        ↓                         ↓
   Business Logic            Integration
        ↓                         ↓
   Unit + Mockito          Real dependency
                                  ↓
                           Testcontainers
                                  ↓
                              API layer
                                  ↓
                           Contract tests
                                  ↓
                             E2E critical flow
```

And always consider:

```text
Happy path
Invalid input
Boundary conditions
Exceptions
Concurrency
Retries
Timeouts
Duplicates
Security
Transactions
Failure recovery
```

For a **7-YOE Java/Spring developer**, testing is not just knowing JUnit annotations. You should be able to explain **why a test belongs at a particular level and what risk that test is protecting against**.

# Part 26 — DevOps, Docker, Kubernetes & CI/CD

## Q861–Q910

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q861. What is DevOps?}}$

**Interview Answer:**

DevOps is a set of practices that brings **development and operations together** to deliver software faster, reliably, and repeatedly through automation.

Typical flow:

```text
Developer
   ↓
Git
   ↓
CI
   ↓
Build
   ↓
Test
   ↓
Security Scan
   ↓
Docker Image
   ↓
Container Registry
   ↓
Deployment
   ↓
Kubernetes / Cloud
   ↓
Monitoring
```

Key principles:

```text
Automation
CI/CD
Infrastructure as Code
Observability
Fast feedback
Reliable deployments
Collaboration
```

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q862. What is CI?}}$

CI = **Continuous Integration**.

Developers frequently merge code into a shared repository, and automated pipelines validate it.

```text
Git Push
   ↓
Build
   ↓
Unit Tests
   ↓
Static Analysis
   ↓
Integration Tests
   ↓
Artifact
```

Goal:

```text
Detect problems early
```

🔥 CI is primarily about **frequent integration + automated validation**.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q863. What is CD?}}$

CD can mean:

### Continuous Delivery

Every change is automatically prepared for release, but production deployment may require approval.

```text
Code
 ↓
Build
 ↓
Test
 ↓
Deploy to staging
 ↓
Approval
 ↓
Production
```

### Continuous Deployment

Successful changes are automatically deployed to production.

```text
Code
 ↓
Build
 ↓
Test
 ↓
Production
```

🔥 Know the distinction in interviews.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q864. What is a CI/CD pipeline for a Spring Boot application?}}$

Example:

```text
Git Push
   ↓
Compile
   ↓
Unit Tests
   ↓
Static Analysis
   ↓
Security Scan
   ↓
Package JAR
   ↓
Build Docker Image
   ↓
Push Registry
   ↓
Deploy
   ↓
Smoke Test
   ↓
Monitor
```

Example Maven build:

```bash
mvn clean verify
```

Then:

```text
target/app.jar
```

is packaged into a container image.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q865. What is Docker?}}$

Docker is a platform for packaging and running applications in isolated containers.

Conceptually:

```text
Application
+
Runtime
+
Dependencies
+
Configuration
        ↓
    Container
```

For Java:

```text
Spring Boot JAR
      +
Java Runtime
      ↓
Docker Image
      ↓
Container
```

Benefits:

```text
Consistency
Isolation
Portability
Fast startup
Easy deployment
```

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q866. What is the difference between a Docker image and container?}}$

### Image

An immutable package/template.

```text
Spring Boot JAR
Java Runtime
Libraries
Metadata
```

### Container

A running instance of an image.

```text
Image
  ↓
Container 1
Container 2
Container 3
```

So:

```text
Image = blueprint
Container = running instance
```

🔥 Multiple containers can be created from the same image.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q867. What is a Dockerfile?}}$

A Dockerfile defines how an image is built.

Example:

```dockerfile
FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre

WORKDIR /app

COPY target/app.jar app.jar

EXPOSE 8080

ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "app.jar"]
```

Flow:

```text
Dockerfile
   ↓
docker build
   ↓
Image
   ↓
docker run
   ↓
Container
```

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q868. What is a multi-stage Docker build?}}$

It uses separate build and runtime stages.

Example:

```dockerfile
FROM maven:3.9-eclipse-temurin-21 AS build

WORKDIR /app

COPY pom.xml .
COPY src ./src

RUN mvn clean package -DskipTests


FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre

WORKDIR /app

COPY --from=build /app/target/app.jar app.jar

ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "app.jar"]
```

Benefits:

```text
Smaller final image
Build tools excluded
Lower attack surface
Cleaner runtime image
```

🔥 Very common production Docker technique.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q869. Why should you avoid running a Java application as root inside a container?}}$

If the application is compromised, root privileges can increase the impact.

Prefer:

```dockerfile
USER appuser
```

with an appropriate non-root user.

Security principle:

```text
Least privilege
```

Other container security considerations:

```text
Minimal base image
No unnecessary packages
Read-only filesystem where practical
Secret management
Image scanning
Non-root execution
```

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q870. What is Docker image layering?}}$

Docker images are composed of layers.

Example:

```text
Base image
   ↓
OS/runtime layer
   ↓
Dependencies
   ↓
Application
```

Docker can reuse unchanged layers.

Therefore ordering Dockerfile instructions carefully can improve build caching.

Example:

```dockerfile
COPY pom.xml .
RUN mvn dependency:go-offline

COPY src ./src
RUN mvn package
```

Dependency changes less frequently than source code, so this can improve build reuse.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q871. What is Kubernetes?}}$

Kubernetes is a container orchestration platform.

It manages:

```text
Deployment
Scaling
Networking
Service discovery
Health checks
Rolling updates
Self-healing
Configuration
```

Conceptually:

```text
                    Kubernetes
                        |
          +-------------+-------------+
          ↓             ↓             ↓
       Pod/App       Pod/App       Pod/App
          |             |             |
        Container     Container     Container
```

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q872. What is a Kubernetes Pod?}}$

A Pod is the smallest deployable unit in Kubernetes.

Usually:

```text
Pod
 └── Container
```

A Pod can contain multiple tightly coupled containers:

```text
Pod
 ├── App Container
 └── Sidecar Container
```

Containers inside the same Pod share:

```text
Network namespace
Pod IP
Volumes where configured
```

🔥 Don't say "Pod = container." A Pod **runs one or more containers**.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q873. Why does Kubernetes use Pods instead of deploying containers directly?}}$

The Pod represents a unit of:

```text
Scheduling
Networking
Storage
Lifecycle
```

Multiple tightly coupled containers can therefore share the same execution context.

Example:

```text
Pod
 ├── Spring Boot app
 └── Supporting sidecar
```

However, don't put unrelated applications into one Pod.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q874. What is a Kubernetes Deployment?}}$

A Deployment manages replicated Pods and their rollout.

```text
Deployment
     ↓
ReplicaSet
     ↓
Pods
```

Example:

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
spec:
  replicas: 3
```

Kubernetes maintains approximately:

```text
3 running replicas
```

It also supports:

```text
Rolling updates
Rollback
Replica management
```

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q875. What is a ReplicaSet?}}$

A ReplicaSet ensures that a specified number of Pod replicas exist.

```text
ReplicaSet
   ↓
Pod
Pod
Pod
```

If one Pod dies:

```text
Pod 1 → DOWN
         ↓
ReplicaSet
         ↓
Create replacement Pod
```

In normal applications, you usually manage ReplicaSets indirectly through Deployments.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q876. What is a Kubernetes Service?}}$

A Service provides a stable network endpoint for a changing set of Pods.

```text
              Service
             /   |   \
            ↓    ↓    ↓
          Pod   Pod   Pod
```

Pods can be replaced and their IPs can change.

The Service provides stable discovery.

Common types:

```text
ClusterIP
NodePort
LoadBalancer
ExternalName
```

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q877. What is ClusterIP?}}$

`ClusterIP` exposes a service inside the Kubernetes cluster.

```text
Order Service
      ↓
ClusterIP
      ↓
Order Pods
```

Other applications inside the cluster can access it.

It is the common default Service type.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q878. What is Ingress?}}$

Ingress provides HTTP/HTTPS routing into Kubernetes.

Example:

```text
Internet
   ↓
Ingress
   ├── /orders → Order Service
   ├── /users  → User Service
   └── /pay    → Payment Service
```

It can provide:

```text
Host routing
Path routing
TLS termination
```

🔥 In modern Kubernetes environments, Gateway API is also increasingly relevant, but Ingress remains a common interview concept.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q879. Ingress vs Service?}}$

### Service

Provides networking to a set of Pods.

```text
Service
 ↓
Pods
```

### Ingress

Routes external HTTP/HTTPS traffic to Services.

```text
Client
 ↓
Ingress
 ↓
Service
 ↓
Pods
```

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q880. What is a ConfigMap?}}$

ConfigMap stores non-sensitive configuration.

Example:

```yaml
data:
  APP_ENV: production
  LOG_LEVEL: INFO
```

Application can consume it as:

```text
Environment variable
File
Configuration source
```

Do not store passwords/secrets in ConfigMaps.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q881. What is a Kubernetes Secret?}}$

Secrets are intended for sensitive configuration.

Examples:

```text
Database password
API credentials
Tokens
Certificates
```

Conceptually:

```text
Secret
  ↓
Pod
  ↓
Spring Boot
```

🔥 Kubernetes Secret is not automatically equivalent to a fully secured enterprise secrets-management solution. Encryption-at-rest and access-control configuration matter.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q882. ConfigMap vs Secret?}}$

| ConfigMap            | Secret           |
| -------------------- | ---------------- |
| Non-sensitive config | Sensitive values |
| Log level            | Password         |
| Feature flag         | Token            |
| Environment config   | Credentials      |

Example:

```text
ConfigMap → LOG_LEVEL=INFO

Secret → DB_PASSWORD=******
```

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q883. What is a Kubernetes liveness probe?}}$

Liveness determines whether a container should be considered unhealthy and restarted.

Example:

```text
Application deadlocked
      ↓
Liveness fails
      ↓
Kubernetes restarts container
```

Spring Boot commonly exposes health endpoints through Actuator.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q884. What is a readiness probe?}}$

Readiness determines whether a Pod should receive traffic.

Example:

```text
Pod starting
   ↓
Not Ready
   ↓
No traffic
   ↓
Dependencies initialized
   ↓
Ready
   ↓
Traffic
```

🔥 Critical distinction:

```text
Liveness
→ Should Kubernetes restart me?

Readiness
→ Should I receive traffic?
```

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q885. What is a startup probe?}}$

A startup probe gives a slow-starting application time to initialize.

```text
Application starts
       ↓
Startup probe
       ↓
Initialization
       ↓
Startup succeeds
       ↓
Liveness/readiness take over
```

Useful for applications with long startup times.

It prevents liveness checks from killing an application while it is still legitimately starting.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q886. How would you configure Spring Boot health checks in Kubernetes?}}$

Use Spring Boot Actuator.

Conceptually:

```text
Kubernetes
    ↓
/actuator/health/liveness
/actuator/health/readiness
```

Example deployment:

```yaml
livenessProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /actuator/health/liveness
    port: 8080

readinessProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /actuator/health/readiness
    port: 8080
```

🔥 Don't make readiness/liveness depend on every external dependency blindly. A temporary downstream outage shouldn't necessarily cause Kubernetes to restart every instance.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q887. What is Kubernetes Horizontal Pod Autoscaler?}}$

HPA automatically changes the number of Pod replicas based on metrics.

```text
Traffic increases
      ↓
CPU / custom metric increases
      ↓
HPA
      ↓
3 Pods → 8 Pods
```

Example:

```yaml
spec:
  minReplicas: 3
  maxReplicas: 10
```

Autoscaling can use CPU/memory and, depending on the setup, custom/external metrics.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q888. Is CPU-based autoscaling always sufficient for Spring Boot?}}$

No.

CPU may not represent the actual bottleneck.

Better signals can include:

```text
Request rate
Latency
Queue depth
Kafka lag
Concurrent requests
Custom business metrics
```

Example:

```text
CPU = 30%
Kafka lag = 1 million messages
```

CPU-based HPA may not scale appropriately.

🔥 Choose scaling metrics based on the workload.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q889. What is a rolling deployment?}}$

A rolling deployment gradually replaces old Pods with new Pods.

```text
Old:
v1 v1 v1

During deployment:
v1 v1 v2

Then:
v1 v2 v2

Finally:
v2 v2 v2
```

Benefits:

```text
Minimal downtime
Gradual rollout
Rollback capability
```

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q890. What is a blue-green deployment?}}$

Two environments:

```text
Blue → Current production
Green → New version
```

Deploy:

```text
Blue = v1
Green = v2
```

Test Green.

Then switch traffic:

```text
Traffic
   ↓
Green v2
```

Rollback:

```text
Traffic
   ↓
Blue v1
```

Advantages:

```text
Fast rollback
Low deployment risk
```

Cost:

```text
Potentially requires duplicate infrastructure
```

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q891. What is a canary deployment?}}$

Release a new version to a small percentage of traffic.

```text
95% → v1
5%  → v2
```

Monitor:

```text
Error rate
Latency
Business metrics
```

Then gradually increase:

```text
5%
 ↓
25%
 ↓
50%
 ↓
100%
```

🔥 Canary is excellent for reducing blast radius.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q892. Rolling vs blue-green vs canary?}}$

| Strategy   | Main Idea                | Benefit              |
| ---------- | ------------------------ | -------------------- |
| Rolling    | Gradually replace Pods   | Simple               |
| Blue-Green | Two environments         | Fast rollback        |
| Canary     | Small traffic percentage | Reduced blast radius |

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q893. What happens when a Kubernetes Pod crashes?}}$

If managed by a Deployment:

```text
Pod crashes
    ↓
Kubernetes detects
    ↓
ReplicaSet/Deployment
    ↓
Replacement Pod
```

But if the application repeatedly crashes:

```text
Crash
 ↓
Restart
 ↓
Crash
 ↓
Restart
```

it may enter:

```text
CrashLoopBackOff
```

🔥 Kubernetes restarts the container, but it cannot fix an application bug.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q894. What is CrashLoopBackOff?}}$

It means a container repeatedly starts and crashes, and Kubernetes backs off before restarting it again.

Possible causes:

```text
Application startup exception
Bad configuration
Missing secret
Port/configuration issue
Dependency failure
OutOfMemoryError
Incorrect command
```

Troubleshooting:

```bash
kubectl logs <pod>
kubectl describe pod <pod>
```

Check:

```text
Previous logs
Events
Environment/config
Resource limits
Probe failures
```

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q895. How would you troubleshoot a Spring Boot Pod that keeps restarting?}}$

My sequence:

```text
1. kubectl get pods

2. kubectl describe pod

3. kubectl logs

4. kubectl logs --previous

5. Check events

6. Check probes

7. Check ConfigMaps/Secrets

8. Check resource limits

9. Check application startup logs

10. Check recent deployment changes
```

For OOM:

```text
Container memory limit
        ↓
JVM memory configuration
        ↓
Heap / Metaspace / native memory
        ↓
GC behavior
```

🔥 Don't blindly increase memory before identifying the cause.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q896. What are Kubernetes resource requests and limits?}}$

### Request

The amount of resource Kubernetes uses when scheduling the Pod.

```yaml
resources:
  requests:
    cpu: "500m"
    memory: "512Mi"
```

### Limit

Maximum resource boundary configured for the container.

```yaml
limits:
  cpu: "1"
  memory: "1Gi"
```

Conceptually:

```text
Request → scheduling expectation
Limit   → upper boundary
```

🔥 Memory limit behavior is especially important because exceeding it can result in an OOM kill.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q897. How do you size JVM memory inside a container?}}$

Don't assume:

```text
-Xmx = container memory
```

because the JVM process also needs memory outside the Java heap.

Consider:

```text
Container memory
 ├── Java heap
 ├── Metaspace
 ├── Thread stacks
 ├── Code cache
 ├── Direct/off-heap memory
 └── Native/runtime overhead
```

Therefore:

```text
Container memory > Xmx
```

with appropriate headroom.

🔥 Modern JVMs are container-aware, but resource sizing still requires measurement.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q898. What is graceful shutdown in Spring Boot/Kubernetes?}}$

During deployment or termination:

```text
Pod receives termination
       ↓
Stop accepting new traffic
       ↓
Allow in-flight requests to finish
       ↓
Close resources
       ↓
Exit
```

Spring Boot supports graceful shutdown configuration.

Kubernetes also provides termination behavior and a grace period.

🔥 This prevents requests from being abruptly terminated during deployments.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q899. What is a Docker health check vs Kubernetes probe?}}$

Docker can define a container health check.

Kubernetes provides:

```text
Liveness
Readiness
Startup
```

In Kubernetes deployments, Kubernetes probes are generally the important application health mechanism.

Remember:

```text
Readiness ≠ Liveness
```

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q900. How should configuration be handled in Spring Boot production?}}$

Avoid hardcoding:

```java
String password = "prodPassword";
```

Instead:

```text
Environment
ConfigMap
Secret
External configuration system
```

Spring Boot:

```text
application.yml
        ↓
Environment
        ↓
@ConfigurationProperties
        ↓
Application
```

Example:

```yaml
spring:
  datasource:
    url: ${DB_URL}
```

🔥 Configuration and secrets should be externalized.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q901. How should secrets be handled in CI/CD?}}$

Never commit:

```text
DB passwords
Private keys
API tokens
Cloud credentials
```

into Git.

Use:

```text
Secret manager
CI/CD secret store
Kubernetes Secrets
Cloud IAM/workload identity
```

Pipeline:

```text
CI/CD
 ↓
Secret provider
 ↓
Deployment
 ↓
Runtime
```

Prefer short-lived credentials/workload identity where supported instead of long-lived static credentials.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q902. What is Infrastructure as Code?}}$

Infrastructure as Code means defining infrastructure using version-controlled configuration/code.

Examples:

```text
Terraform
CloudFormation
Pulumi
Ansible
Kubernetes manifests
Helm
```

Instead of manually creating:

```text
Servers
Networks
Load balancers
Databases
```

you define them declaratively.

Benefits:

```text
Repeatability
Version control
Automation
Reviewability
Consistency
```

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q903. What is Helm in Kubernetes?}}$

Helm is a package manager/template system commonly used for Kubernetes applications.

Instead of maintaining many duplicated YAML files:

```text
deployment-dev.yaml
deployment-test.yaml
deployment-prod.yaml
```

you can parameterize templates.

Conceptually:

```text
Helm Chart
   +
values.yaml
   ↓
Kubernetes manifests
```

Example:

```text
replicaCount: 3
image:
  tag: "1.4.2"
```

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q904. What is the difference between Kubernetes Deployment and StatefulSet?}}$

### Deployment

For mostly stateless applications:

```text
Spring Boot API
```

Pods are replaceable.

### StatefulSet

For stateful workloads requiring stable identity/storage semantics.

Examples:

```text
Certain databases
Kafka deployments
Stateful distributed systems
```

Provides concepts such as:

```text
Stable Pod identity
Stable network identity
Persistent storage association
Ordered deployment/scaling semantics
```

🔥 Don't deploy every stateful database blindly inside Kubernetes just because Kubernetes supports StatefulSets.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q905. What is a PersistentVolume?}}$

PersistentVolume provides persistent storage to Kubernetes workloads.

Conceptually:

```text
Pod
 ↓
PersistentVolumeClaim
 ↓
PersistentVolume
 ↓
Storage
```

If a Pod is recreated:

```text
Pod dies
 ↓
New Pod
 ↓
Same persistent storage
```

when correctly configured.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q906. How would you deploy a Spring Boot application with zero/minimal downtime?}}$

Use:

```text
Multiple replicas
+
Readiness probe
+
Rolling deployment
+
Graceful shutdown
+
Load balancing
```

Flow:

```text
v1 Pods
  ↓
Deploy v2
  ↓
v2 Pod starts
  ↓
Readiness passes
  ↓
Traffic → v2
  ↓
Terminate v1 gradually
```

🔥 Readiness is critical. A newly started but not-ready Pod should not receive traffic.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q907. What would you include in a production CI/CD pipeline for Spring Boot?}}$

A strong pipeline:

```text
Git Push
   ↓
Compile
   ↓
Unit Tests
   ↓
Static Analysis
   ↓
Dependency/SAST scanning
   ↓
Integration Tests
   ↓
Package JAR
   ↓
Build Image
   ↓
Image Scan
   ↓
Push Registry
   ↓
Deploy Dev
   ↓
Smoke Tests
   ↓
Deploy Staging
   ↓
Contract/E2E Tests
   ↓
Approval / automated promotion
   ↓
Production
   ↓
Health + Metrics
```

For production:

```text
Canary / Rolling
+
Rollback
+
Observability
```

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q908. What is rollback in CI/CD?}}$

Rollback means returning to a previously known-good version.

Example:

```text
v1 → stable

Deploy v2
 ↓
Error rate increases
 ↓
Rollback
 ↓
v1
```

Good deployments keep:

```text
Previous image
Previous configuration
Deployment history
```

🔥 Database rollback is harder than application rollback. Schema migrations should therefore be designed carefully for backward compatibility.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q909. What would you do if a production deployment suddenly causes 5× more errors?}}$

My incident approach:

```text
1. Detect
2. Confirm impact
3. Check recent deployment
4. Compare v1 vs v2 metrics
5. Stop rollout
6. Roll back if appropriate
7. Preserve evidence
8. Investigate root cause
9. Fix
10. Redeploy safely
```

Check:

```text
Error rate
Latency
Logs
Traces
CPU
Memory
DB
Kafka
External dependencies
```

🔥 During an incident, **restore service first**, then perform deeper root-cause analysis.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q910. Design the complete production deployment architecture for a Spring Boot microservice.}}$

🔥🔥 **Capstone DevOps question.**

```text
                         Developer
                             |
                            Git
                             |
                         CI Pipeline
                             |
       +---------------------+--------------------+
       |                     |                    |
    Unit Tests          Security Scan       Integration
       |                     |                 Tests
       +---------------------+--------------------+
                             |
                       Build JAR/Image
                             |
                       Image Registry
                             |
                         CD Pipeline
                             |
                         Kubernetes
                             |
                    +--------+--------+
                    |                 |
                 Ingress          Service
                    |                 |
                    +--------+--------+
                             |
                      Spring Boot Pods
                    +--------+--------+
                    |        |        |
                   Pod      Pod      Pod
                    |        |        |
                    +--------+--------+
                             |
          +------------------+------------------+
          |                  |                  |
        Redis              Kafka               DB
          |                  |                  |
       Cache            Event Stream        Persistent
                                             Storage
```

### Application layer

```text
Ingress
   ↓
Service
   ↓
Spring Boot
   ↓
Controller
   ↓
Service
   ↓
Repository
   ↓
Database
```

### Deployment reliability

```text
Rolling / Canary
       ↓
Readiness
       ↓
Graceful Shutdown
       ↓
Health Monitoring
       ↓
Rollback
```

### Scaling

```text
Traffic
  ↓
HPA
  ↓
More Pods
```

### Security

```text
Non-root container
Minimal image
Image scanning
Secrets management
TLS
RBAC
Network policies where appropriate
Least privilege
```

### Observability

```text
Logs
Metrics
Traces
Health
Alerts
```

### Failure handling

```text
Pod crash
 → Kubernetes restarts

Pod unhealthy
 → Readiness removes traffic

Traffic spike
 → HPA scales

Deployment bad
 → Rollback

DB slow
 → Metrics + traces + DB monitoring

Kafka lag
 → Consumer metrics + scaling

Redis unavailable
 → Application fallback/degraded behavior
```

# Part 27 — AWS & Cloud for Java/Spring 7-YOE

## Q911–Q960

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q911. What is cloud computing?}}$

**Interview Answer:**

Cloud computing provides computing resources such as:

```text
Compute
Storage
Database
Networking
Messaging
Security
Monitoring
```

on demand over the internet, usually with usage-based pricing.

Instead of:

```text
Company Data Center
   ↓
Buy Servers
   ↓
Install/maintain hardware
```

we can use:

```text
AWS
 ↓
Provision resources
 ↓
Deploy application
```

Major cloud models:

```text
IaaS
PaaS
SaaS
```

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q912. What is IaaS vs PaaS vs SaaS?}}$

### IaaS — Infrastructure as a Service

You manage more of the infrastructure.

Example:

```text
EC2
```

You manage:

```text
OS
Application
Runtime
Configuration
```

### PaaS — Platform as a Service

Cloud provider manages more infrastructure.

Examples can include managed application platforms and databases.

### SaaS — Software as a Service

You consume a complete software product.

Example:

```text
Gmail
Salesforce
```

Mental model:

```text
IaaS → more control
PaaS → less infrastructure management
SaaS → consume finished software
```

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q913. What is AWS?}}$

AWS is Amazon's cloud computing platform providing services for:

```text
Compute
Storage
Databases
Networking
Security
Messaging
Containers
Monitoring
AI/ML
Serverless
```

For a Java/Spring developer, important services include:

```text
EC2
EKS
ECS
RDS
S3
ElastiCache
ALB
SQS
SNS
MSK
IAM
CloudWatch
Secrets Manager
Route 53
CloudFront
```

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q914. What is an AWS Region?}}$

A Region is a geographic AWS location containing multiple Availability Zones.

Example concept:

```text
AWS Region
 ├── AZ-A
 ├── AZ-B
 └── AZ-C
```

Applications can be deployed across multiple AZs for higher availability.

🔥 Don't confuse Region with Availability Zone.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q915. What is an Availability Zone?}}$

An Availability Zone is an isolated location within an AWS Region designed to provide fault isolation.

Example:

```text
Region
 ├── AZ-1
 │    ├── App
 │    └── DB replica
 │
 ├── AZ-2
 │    ├── App
 │    └── DB
 │
 └── AZ-3
      └── App
```

Deploying multiple application instances across AZs reduces the impact of an AZ failure.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q916. Region vs Availability Zone?}}$

| Region                       | Availability Zone               |
| ---------------------------- | ------------------------------- |
| Geographic AWS area          | Isolated location within Region |
| Contains multiple AZs        | Belongs to one Region           |
| Used for regional deployment | Used for fault isolation        |

Example:

```text
Region
   ↓
AZ-A + AZ-B + AZ-C
```

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q917. What is AWS VPC?}}$

VPC = Virtual Private Cloud.

It provides an isolated logical network in AWS.

Conceptually:

```text
AWS
 |
 VPC
 |
 +---------------------------+
 |                           |
 | Public Subnet      Private Subnet
 |                           |
 | ALB                    App
 |                        |
 |                       DB
 +---------------------------+
```

You define:

```text
IP ranges
Subnets
Routing
Security
Network connectivity
```

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q918. What is a subnet?}}$

A subnet is a subdivision of a VPC IP address range.

Common architecture:

```text
VPC
 |
 +-- Public Subnet
 |
 +-- Private App Subnet
 |
 +-- Private DB Subnet
```

Typical principle:

```text
Internet-facing resources
→ Public subnet

Internal application/database
→ Private subnet
```

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q919. What makes a subnet public or private?}}$

The key distinction is routing.

A public subnet has a route through an Internet Gateway for internet connectivity.

Example:

```text
Public subnet
      ↓
Internet Gateway
      ↓
Internet
```

A private subnet does not have a direct route to the internet through an Internet Gateway.

For outbound internet access, private resources can use:

```text
Private subnet
      ↓
NAT Gateway
      ↓
Internet Gateway
      ↓
Internet
```

🔥 A subnet isn't "public" simply because its IP range is public/private; routing determines the behavior.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q920. What is an Internet Gateway?}}$

An Internet Gateway provides connectivity between a VPC and the public internet.

Conceptually:

```text
Internet
   ↕
Internet Gateway
   ↕
Public Subnet
```

Resources also need appropriate routing and public addressing to communicate with the internet.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q921. What is a NAT Gateway?}}$

NAT Gateway allows resources in private subnets to initiate outbound connections to the internet without allowing unsolicited inbound internet connections directly to those resources.

Example:

```text
Private Spring Boot
       ↓
NAT Gateway
       ↓
Internet
```

Useful for:

```text
Package downloads
External APIs
Updates
Outbound connections
```

🔥 NAT Gateway is primarily for outbound connectivity from private networks.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q922. What is AWS Security Group?}}$

A Security Group acts as a virtual firewall for supported AWS resources.

Rules control:

```text
Inbound traffic
Outbound traffic
```

Example:

```text
Internet
   ↓ 443
ALB Security Group
   ↓ 8080
App Security Group
   ↓ 5432
DB Security Group
```

This creates layered access control.

🔥 Security Groups are stateful.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q923. What is a Network ACL?}}$

A Network ACL (NACL) is a subnet-level network access control mechanism.

Compared conceptually:

```text
Security Group
→ Resource-level

NACL
→ Subnet-level
```

NACL rules are stateless, so return traffic must be explicitly allowed as needed.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q924. Security Group vs NACL?}}$

| Security Group                       | NACL                              |
| ------------------------------------ | --------------------------------- |
| Resource-level                       | Subnet-level                      |
| Stateful                             | Stateless                         |
| Primarily allow rules                | Allow and deny rules              |
| Return traffic automatically handled | Return traffic must be considered |

Typical architecture:

```text
Internet
 ↓
ALB SG
 ↓
App SG
 ↓
DB SG
```

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q925. What is AWS EC2?}}$

EC2 = Elastic Compute Cloud.

It provides virtual servers.

For Java:

```text
EC2
 ↓
Linux
 ↓
Java
 ↓
Spring Boot
 ↓
8080
```

You manage much of:

```text
OS
Runtime
Application
Patching
Scaling strategy
```

Compared with managed platforms, EC2 gives more control but more operational responsibility.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q926. How would you deploy a Spring Boot application on EC2?}}$

Basic architecture:

```text
Internet
   ↓
Route 53
   ↓
ALB
   ↓
EC2
   ↓
Spring Boot
```

For production:

```text
                 ALB
              /       \
           EC2-A      EC2-B
              \       /
               RDS
```

Use:

```text
Auto Scaling Group
CloudWatch
IAM Role
Secrets Manager
Private subnets where appropriate
```

Avoid exposing application EC2 instances directly to the internet when an ALB architecture can provide the required boundary.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q927. What is an AMI?}}$

AMI = Amazon Machine Image.

It is a template used to launch EC2 instances.

Conceptually:

```text
AMI
 ↓
EC2 Instance
```

An AMI can contain:

```text
OS
Installed software
Configuration
Application artifacts
```

Modern deployment pipelines often build immutable images rather than manually configuring servers after launch.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q928. What is an Auto Scaling Group?}}$

An Auto Scaling Group manages a group of EC2 instances.

```text
ASG
 ├── EC2
 ├── EC2
 └── EC2
```

If traffic increases:

```text
3 → 6 instances
```

If demand decreases:

```text
6 → 3 instances
```

It can also replace unhealthy instances.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q929. What is an Application Load Balancer?}}$

ALB distributes HTTP/HTTPS traffic across targets.

```text
                 ALB
               /     \
             EC2     EC2
```

It supports features such as:

```text
Path-based routing
Host-based routing
TLS termination
Health checks
```

Example:

```text
/api/orders → Order Service
/api/users  → User Service
```

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q930. ALB vs NLB?}}$

### ALB

Layer-7 HTTP/HTTPS load balancer.

Good for:

```text
HTTP
HTTPS
Path routing
Host routing
Web applications
REST APIs
```

### NLB

Layer-4 load balancer.

Useful when:

```text
TCP
UDP
Very high performance
Low-level network traffic
```

🔥 Choose based on protocol and routing requirements, not simply "NLB is faster."

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q931. What is AWS RDS?}}$

RDS is a managed relational database service.

Supports database engines such as:

```text
PostgreSQL
MySQL
MariaDB
Oracle
SQL Server
```

AWS manages infrastructure tasks such as:

```text
Provisioning
Backups
Patching
High availability options
Monitoring
```

You still manage:

```text
Schema
Queries
Indexes
Application transactions
Database design
```

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q932. What is Multi-AZ RDS?}}$

Multi-AZ provides a high-availability deployment across Availability Zones.

Conceptually:

```text
Application
    ↓
RDS
 ├── Primary
 └── Standby
```

If the primary fails, AWS can perform failover to the standby.

🔥 Multi-AZ is primarily about **availability**, not automatically about read scaling.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q933. RDS Multi-AZ vs Read Replica?}}$

### Multi-AZ

Primary purpose:

```text
High Availability
Failover
```

### Read Replica

Primary purpose:

```text
Read scaling
```

Conceptually:

```text
                Primary
               /       \
          Standby      Read Replica
          (HA)          (Reads)
```

🔥 This distinction is commonly asked.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q934. What is AWS S3?}}$

S3 = Simple Storage Service.

It is object storage.

Good for:

```text
Images
Documents
Videos
Backups
Logs
Static assets
Large files
```

Conceptually:

```text
Spring Boot
    ↓
S3
    ↓
Object
```

Don't use a relational DB BLOB column automatically just because it can store files.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q935. How would you upload a large file to S3 from a Spring Boot application?}}$

Prefer a pre-signed URL approach.

```text
Client
   ↓
Spring Boot
   ↓
Generate pre-signed URL
   ↓
Client
   ↓
S3
```

The application server doesn't have to proxy the entire file.

Benefits:

```text
Lower application bandwidth
Better scalability
Reduced memory pressure
Direct S3 upload
```

For very large objects, multipart upload can be used.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q936. What is an S3 pre-signed URL?}}$

A pre-signed URL grants temporary access to an S3 operation.

Example:

```text
Spring Boot
    ↓
Generate temporary URL
    ↓
Client
    ↓
S3
```

The client can upload/download without receiving permanent AWS credentials.

🔥 Use short expiration times and appropriate permissions.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q937. What is AWS ElastiCache?}}$

ElastiCache provides managed in-memory caching services such as:

```text
Redis
Memcached
```

For Spring Boot:

```text
Spring Boot
    ↓
Redis
    ↓
Cache
```

Use cases:

```text
Caching
Sessions
Counters
Rate limiting
Distributed coordination where appropriate
```

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q938. What is AWS IAM?}}$

IAM = Identity and Access Management.

It controls:

```text
Who can access what
What actions are allowed
Which resources can be accessed
```

Core concepts:

```text
Users
Roles
Policies
Groups
```

For applications, prefer IAM roles over embedding long-lived AWS access keys.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q939. What is an IAM Role?}}$

An IAM Role provides permissions that can be assumed by trusted entities.

Example:

```text
EC2
 ↓
IAM Role
 ↓
S3:GetObject
```

The application doesn't need a hardcoded AWS access key.

Similarly:

```text
EKS Pod
 ↓
Workload identity mechanism
 ↓
AWS permissions
```

🔥 Prefer temporary credentials/roles over static credentials.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q940. What is the principle of least privilege in AWS?}}$

Give an identity only the permissions it needs.

Bad:

```text
Application
→ AdministratorAccess
```

Better:

```text
Order Service
→ Read/write specific S3 bucket
```

Example:

```text
s3:GetObject
s3:PutObject
```

only where required.

🔥 Least privilege should apply to applications, CI/CD, developers, and infrastructure.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q941. What is AWS Secrets Manager?}}$

Secrets Manager securely stores sensitive values.

Examples:

```text
DB password
API key
OAuth secret
Credentials
```

Spring Boot can retrieve secrets through application configuration/integration mechanisms.

Instead of:

```yaml
password: myPassword123
```

use:

```text
Secret Manager
      ↓
Application
```

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q942. Secrets Manager vs Parameter Store?}}$

### Secrets Manager

Designed specifically for secrets.

Features can include:

```text
Secret storage
Access control
Rotation capabilities
```

### Parameter Store

Stores configuration parameters and can also securely store encrypted values depending on parameter type/configuration.

Typical distinction:

```text
Normal configuration
→ Parameter Store

Sensitive credentials/secrets
→ Secrets Manager
```

But actual choice depends on requirements and AWS features used.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q943. What is CloudWatch?}}$

CloudWatch provides AWS monitoring and observability capabilities.

It can collect:

```text
Metrics
Logs
Events
Alarms
```

Example:

```text
Spring Boot / EC2
       ↓
CloudWatch
       ↓
Metrics + Logs + Alarms
```

Useful metrics:

```text
CPU
Memory where configured
Request count
Latency
Errors
Instance health
```

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q944. How would you monitor a Spring Boot application on AWS?}}$

Use multiple layers:

```text
Application
 ↓
Spring Boot Actuator
 ↓
Metrics
 ↓
CloudWatch / Prometheus
 ↓
Dashboards + Alerts
```

Also:

```text
ALB metrics
EC2/EKS metrics
RDS metrics
Redis metrics
Kafka metrics
Distributed tracing
Centralized logs
```

Monitor:

```text
RPS
p95/p99 latency
Error rate
CPU
Memory
GC
DB pool
DB latency
Kafka lag
Cache hit ratio
```

🔥 Monitor business metrics too.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q945. What is AWS SQS?}}$

SQS = Simple Queue Service.

It is a managed message queue.

Conceptually:

```text
Producer
   ↓
SQS
   ↓
Consumer
```

Useful for:

```text
Asynchronous processing
Work queues
Decoupling
Retry handling
Traffic smoothing
```

Example:

```text
Order Service
    ↓
SQS
    ↓
Email Worker
```

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q946. What is AWS SNS?}}$

SNS = Simple Notification Service.

It is a publish/subscribe messaging service.

Conceptually:

```text
Publisher
    ↓
SNS Topic
   / | \
  ↓  ↓  ↓
SQS Lambda Email/etc.
```

It is useful when one event needs to fan out to multiple subscribers.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q947. SQS vs SNS?}}$

### SQS

Queue:

```text
Producer
   ↓
Queue
   ↓
Consumer
```

### SNS

Pub/Sub:

```text
Publisher
   ↓
Topic
 ├── SQS
 ├── Lambda
 └── other subscribers
```

Mental model:

```text
SQS → work queue
SNS → fan-out notification
```

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q948. What is Amazon MSK?}}$

Amazon MSK = Managed Streaming for Apache Kafka.

It provides managed Kafka infrastructure.

Architecture:

```text
Spring Boot Producer
       ↓
      MSK
       ↓
Spring Boot Consumers
```

AWS manages much of the Kafka infrastructure, while you still need to understand:

```text
Topics
Partitions
Replication
Consumer groups
Offsets
Retention
Lag
Producer/consumer configuration
```

🔥 Managed Kafka does not remove Kafka architecture responsibilities.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q949. SQS vs Kafka/MSK?}}$

### SQS

Good for:

```text
Work queue
Simple asynchronous processing
Managed queue semantics
```

### Kafka/MSK

Good for:

```text
Event streaming
High-throughput event pipelines
Replay
Multiple independent consumer groups
Partition-based ordering
```

Conceptually:

```text
SQS:
Message → consumed/removed according to queue semantics

Kafka:
Record → retained according to retention policy
         ↓
Multiple consumer groups can replay/read independently
```

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q950. What is Route 53?}}$

Route 53 is AWS's DNS service.

Example:

```text
api.example.com
       ↓
Route 53
       ↓
ALB
       ↓
Spring Boot
```

It can support:

```text
DNS routing
Health checks
Traffic policies
Domain management
```

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q951. What is CloudFront?}}$

CloudFront is AWS's CDN.

Conceptually:

```text
User
 ↓
CloudFront Edge
 ↓
Origin
```

Useful for:

```text
Static files
Images
Videos
Cacheable content
Global content delivery
```

Example:

```text
User in India
   ↓
Nearest suitable edge location
   ↓
Cached image
```

This reduces latency and origin load.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q952. What is AWS EKS?}}$

EKS = Elastic Kubernetes Service.

It provides managed Kubernetes control-plane capabilities.

Architecture:

```text
AWS
 |
EKS
 |
 +-- Kubernetes
      |
      +-- Pods
      +-- Services
      +-- Deployments
```

You can deploy Spring Boot containers to EKS.

```text
Docker Image
     ↓
ECR
     ↓
EKS
     ↓
Spring Boot Pods
```

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q953. What is AWS ECS?}}$

ECS = Elastic Container Service.

It is AWS's container orchestration service.

Common architecture:

```text
ECS
 ↓
Service
 ↓
Tasks
 ↓
Spring Boot Container
```

ECS can run tasks using launch models such as:

```text
EC2
Fargate
```

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q954. ECS vs EKS?}}$

### ECS

AWS-native container orchestration.

```text
Simpler AWS-specific approach
```

### EKS

Managed Kubernetes.

```text
Kubernetes ecosystem
Portability
Kubernetes APIs/tools
```

Choose based on:

```text
Team expertise
Existing platform
Portability requirements
Operational complexity
AWS integration
```

🔥 Don't say EKS is automatically better because it is Kubernetes.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q955. What is AWS Fargate?}}$

Fargate is a serverless compute option for running containers without directly managing the underlying servers.

Conceptually:

```text
Docker Image
     ↓
ECS/Fargate
     ↓
Container
```

You specify resources such as:

```text
CPU
Memory
```

and AWS manages the underlying compute infrastructure.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q956. What is ECR?}}$

ECR = Elastic Container Registry.

It stores Docker/container images.

Typical pipeline:

```text
Developer
   ↓
CI
   ↓
Docker Build
   ↓
ECR
   ↓
ECS / EKS
```

Example:

```text
my-service:1.4.2
```

is stored in ECR.

🔥 Image scanning and immutable versioning/tagging strategies are important production considerations.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q957. How would you deploy a production Spring Boot application on AWS?}}$

One possible architecture:

```text
                         Internet
                            |
                       Route 53
                            |
                       CloudFront
                            |
                      API Gateway/ALB
                            |
                    +-------+-------+
                    |               |
                  EKS             EKS
                Pods            Pods
                    |               |
                    +-------+-------+
                            |
             +--------------+--------------+
             |              |              |
           Redis           Kafka           RDS
        ElastiCache         MSK          Multi-AZ
             |              |              |
             +--------------+--------------+
                            |
                           S3
```

Deployment:

```text
Git
 ↓
CI
 ↓
Tests + Security Scan
 ↓
Docker Build
 ↓
ECR
 ↓
EKS
 ↓
Rolling/Canary Deployment
```

Security:

```text
IAM
Security Groups
Private subnets
Secrets Manager
TLS
Least privilege
```

Observability:

```text
CloudWatch
Metrics
Logs
Tracing
Alerts
Actuator
```

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q958. How would you design a highly available Spring Boot system on AWS?}}$

Use multiple Availability Zones.

```text
                    ALB
                 /       \
               AZ-A      AZ-B
                |          |
             App Pods    App Pods
                \          /
                 \        /
                    RDS
                  Multi-AZ
```

Also:

```text
Redis HA
Kafka replication
Multiple application instances
Auto Scaling
Health checks
Backups
Monitoring
```

Avoid:

```text
Single EC2
Single DB
Single AZ
Single application instance
```

🔥 High availability is about eliminating critical single points of failure.

---

### $\color{red}{\text{Q959. What happens if one AWS Availability Zone fails?}}$

With a properly distributed architecture:

```text
AZ-A → DOWN

ALB
 ↓
AZ-B
 ↓
Healthy application instances
```

Database:

```text
Multi-AZ RDS
 ↓
Failover
```

The system may continue serving traffic with reduced capacity.

However, this depends on:

```text
Architecture
Capacity
Health checks
Database configuration
Application dependencies
```

🔥 Multi-AZ improves resilience; it doesn't guarantee zero impact for every failure.

---

# ⭐ AWS Mental Model for a Java Developer

You don't need to memorize AWS as hundreds of isolated services.

Think in layers:

```text
                    AWS
                     |
        +------------+------------+
        |            |            |
      Network      Compute      Storage
        |            |            |
       VPC        EKS/ECS/EC2     S3
       ALB            |
       Route53    Spring Boot
        |             |
        +-------------+-------------+
                      |
                  Data Layer
                 /    |    \
               RDS  Redis  Kafka
                 \    |    /
                  Spring Boot
                      |
                  Security
                      |
              IAM / Secrets / TLS
                      |
                Observability
                      |
               CloudWatch/Tracing
                      |
                    CI/CD
                      |
                 Git → ECR → EKS
```

The key interview principle is:

> **Don't answer AWS questions by listing services. Explain why you chose each service, what problem it solves, what happens when it fails, and what trade-off it introduces.**
